Log-concavity and log-convexity via distributive lattices

Jinting Liang Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of British Columbia, Affiliation: 1984 Mathematics Rd, Vancouver, BC V6T 1Z2, CANADA, liangj@math.ubc.ca Affiliation: and Affiliation: Bruce E. Sagan (corresponding author) Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Michigan State University, Affiliation: East Lansing, MI 48824-1027, USA, bsagan@msu.edu
September 14, 2026
Key Words: Catalan numbers, descent polynomial, distributive lattice, FKG inequality, lattice path, log-concavity, log-convexity, Lucas sequence, noncrossing partition, order ideal, peak polynomial, permutation pattern, Schur function, set partition, Stirling number, Young’s lattice
AMS subject classification (2020): 05A20 (Primary) 05A05, 05A10, 05A18, 06D99 (Secondary)
Abstract

The FKG inequality is a powerful tool for proving inequalities in distributive lattices. We show how a special case, which we call the Order Ideal Lemma, can be used to demonstrate a wide array of log-concavity and log-convexity results in a combinatorial manner. We use the Order Ideal Lemma to prove log-concavity and log-convexity of various sequences involving lattice paths (Catalan, Motzkin and large Schröder numbers), intervals in Young’s lattice, order polynomials, specializations of Schur and Schur QQ-functions, Lucas sequences, descent and peak polynomials of permutations, pattern avoidance, set partitions, and noncrossing partitions. We end with a section with conjectures and outlining future directions.

1 Introduction

Let

(an)n≥0=a0,a1,a2,…(a_{n})_{n\geq 0}=a_{0},a_{1},a_{2},\ldots

be a sequence of real numbers. The sequence is log-concave if

an2≥an−1​an+1a_{n}^{2}\geq a_{n-1}a_{n+1} (1)

for all n≥1n\geq 1. A log-convex sequence is one satisfying

an2≤an−1​an+1a_{n}^{2}\leq a_{n-1}a_{n+1} (2)

for all n≥1n\geq 1. Log-concave and log-convex sequences abound in combinatorics, algebra, and geometry. See the survey articles of Stanley [Sta89], Brenti [Bre94], and Brändén [Br15] for more information. By specialization of the FKG inequality [FKG71], we obtain a combinatorial tool for proving log-concavity and log-convexity using order ideals in distributive lattices. We then apply this method to obtain a host of such results both old and new in a unified way.

Let us review some basic concepts from the theory of partially ordered sets (posets). More comprehensive treatments can be found in the books of Sagan [Sag20] or Stanley [Sta12]. All of our posets will be finite. A lower order ideal in a poset (P,⪯)(P,\preceq) is I⊆PI\subseteq P such that if x∈Ix\in I and y⪯xy\preceq x then y∈Iy\in I. Similarly, an upper order ideal is J⊆PJ\subseteq P satisfying x∈Jx\in J and y⪰xy\succeq x implies y∈Jy\in J. We will use “order ideal” to refer to a subset which could be either. Say that poset LL is a lattice if every pair x,y∈Lx,y\in L has a greatest lower bound or meet, x∧yx\wedge y, as well as a least upper bound or join, x∨yx\vee y. The lattice is distributive if it satisfies either of the two equivalent distributive laws that, for all x,y,z∈Lx,y,z\in L,

x∧(y∨z)=(x∧y)∨(x∧z)x\wedge(y\vee z)=(x\wedge y)\vee(x\wedge z)

and

x∨(y∧z)=(x∨y)∧(x∨z).x\vee(y\wedge z)=(x\vee y)\wedge(x\vee z).

We can now state our fundamental result which we call the Order Ideal Lemma. It is an easy consequence of the FKG Inequality [FKG71]. But since its proof involves concepts not needed in the rest of this paper, we postpone the demonstration until Subsection 8.1. For a set SS we will use both |S||S| and #​S\#S for its cardinality.

Lemma 1.1 (The Order Ideal Lemma).

Let LL be a distributive lattice and suppose that I,J⊆LI,J\subseteq L are ideals.

  1. (a)

    If I,JI,J are both lower ideals or both upper ideals then

    |I|⋅|J|≤|I∩J|⋅|L|.|I|\cdot|J|\leq|I\cap J|\cdot|L|.
  2. (b)

    If one of I,JI,J is a lower order ideal and the other is upper then

    |I|⋅|J|≥|I∩J|⋅|L|.|I|\cdot|J|\geq|I\cap J|\cdot|L|.

We note that part (a) of the Order Ideal Lemma appeared in a paper of Daykin, Kleitman, and West [DKW79, equation (2)]. But it’s wide applicability does not seem to have been previously recognized.

Our general strategy for proving log-convexity of a sequence (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} will be to construct lattices LnL_{n} with |Ln|=an|L_{n}|=a_{n}. If we can find inside Ln+1L_{n+1} two lower order ideals I,JI,J such that |I|=|J|=an|I|=|J|=a_{n} and |I∩J|=an−1|I\cap J|=a_{n-1} then we will be done by part (a) of the Order Ideal Lemma. Similarly, part (b) can be used to prove log-concavity.

The rest of this paper is structured as follows. In the next section we will use lattice paths to prove log-convexity of sequences involving the Catalan, Motzkin, and large Schröder numbers. In Section 3 we use various intervals in Young’s lattice to give log-concavity and log-convexity results. Some of these specialize to the fact that show that various sequences of binomial coefficients are log-concave. We begin Section 4 by showing that for any poset, the sequence obtained by evaluating its (enriched) order polynomial at nonnegative integers is always log-concave. As a consequence, we obtain log-concavity of sequences of specializations of Schur and Schur QQ-functions. Section 5 is dedicated to generalized Lucas sequences which are those satisfying an=an−1+an−2a_{n}=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2} for n≥2n\geq 2. We show that any such sequence which has positive initial conditions alternates between satisfying (1) and (2). In Section 6 we consider various sequences related to permutations, including those defined by pattern avoidance as well as sequences of descent and peak polynomials. The focus of Section 7 is set partitions and we show log-concavity of sequences involving Stirling numbers of the second kind and Narayana numbers. The last section contains a proof of the Order Ideal Lemma as well as directions for future research.

2 Lattice paths

In this section we will use lattice paths together with the Order Ideal Lemma to give unified proofs of the log-convexity of the sequences of Catalan, Motzkin, and large Schröder numbers. We begin with a review of some basic definitions.

A lattice path is a sequence P:p0,p1,…,pnP:p_{0},p_{1},\ldots,p_{n} of points in the integer lattice so pi∈ℤ2p_{i}\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{2} for all ii. A step of PP is the vector [xi,yi][x_{i},y_{i}] from pi−1p_{i-1} to pip_{i}. When the initial vertex p0p_{0} of PP is known, we can specify PP by listing its steps. An up step is a step U=[1,1]U=[1,1] and a down step is D=[1,−1]D=[1,-1]. A Dyck path of semilength nn is a lattice path PP satisfying

  1. 1.

    PP starts at p0=(0,0)p_{0}=(0,0) and ends at p2​n=(2​n,0)p_{2n}=(2n,0),

  2. 2.

    PP uses steps UU and DD and never goes below the xx-axis.

Figure 1 displays the five Dyck paths of semilength 33. Let

𝒟n={P∣P is a Dyck path of semilength n}.{\cal D}_{n}=\{P\mid\text{$P$ is a Dyck path of semilength $n$}\}.

It is well known that the cardinality of 𝒟n{\cal D}_{n} is the Catalan number

Cn=1n+1​(2​nn).C_{n}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}. (3)

We wish to turn 𝒟n{\cal D}_{n} into a distributive lattice. If P∈𝒟nP\in{\cal D}_{n} then we let A⁡(P)A(P) be the area of PP which is the set of all points of ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2} between PP and the xx-axis. In Figure 1 the areas are shaded. We now define a partial order on 𝒟n{\cal D}_{n} by

P⪯Q​ if and only if ​A​(P)⊆A⁡(Q).P\preceq Q\text{ if and only if }A(P)\subseteq A(Q). (4)

The Hasse diagram for 𝒟3{\cal D}_{3} is in Figure 1. We note that 𝒟n{\cal D}_{n} is a distributive lattice. This follows from the fact that it is isomorphic to an interval in Young’s lattice and we will discuss various interesting intervals in the next section. It is also a consequence of a more general theorem of Ferrari and Pinzani [FP05] giving a criterion for a family of lattice paths ordered by (4) to be a distributive lattice. The next result follows from easy algebraic manipulations of (3). But our proof is combinatorial and will generalize to other families of paths where a closed-form formula is not known. We note that a qq-analogue of this result has been proved by Butler and Flanigan [BF07], although it does not use the standard definition of qq-log convexity discussed in Subsection 8.3 below.

Theorem 2.1.

The sequence (Cn)n≥0(C_{n})_{n\geq 0} of Catalan numbers is log-convex.

Proof.

We begin with the distributive lattice 𝒟n+1{\cal D}_{n+1} and note that |𝒟n+1|=Cn+1|{\cal D}_{n+1}|=C_{n+1}.

Let

I={P∈𝒟n+1∣P=U​D​P′ for some translated Dyck path P′ of semilength n}.I=\{P\in{\cal D}_{n+1}\mid\text{$P=UDP^{\prime}$ for some translated Dyck path $P^{\prime}$ of semilength $n$}\}.

it follows that II is a lower order ideal because if P∈IP\in I and Q⪯PQ\preceq P then (4) forces Q=U​D​Q′Q=UDQ^{\prime} for some Q′Q^{\prime}. Furthermore, we have an isomorphism of posets I≅𝒟nI\cong{\cal D}_{n} given by P=U​D​P′↦P′P=UDP^{\prime}\mapsto P^{\prime}. Thus |I|=Cn|I|=C_{n}.

Now consider

J={P∈𝒟n+1∣P=P′​U​D for some Dyck path P′ of semilength n}.J=\{P\in{\cal D}_{n+1}\mid\text{$P=P^{\prime}UD$ for some Dyck path $P^{\prime}$ of semilength $n$}\}.

Similar considerations to those in the previous paragraph show that |J|=Cn|J|=C_{n}. Furthermore

I∩J={P∈𝒟n+1∣P=U​D​P′​U​D for some Dyck path P′ of semilength n−1}I\cap J=\{P\in{\cal D}_{n+1}\mid\text{$P=UDP^{\prime}UD$ for some Dyck path $P^{\prime}$ of semilength $n-1$}\}

so that |I∩J|=Cn−1|I\cap J|=C_{n-1}. Now applying part (a) of the Order Ideal Lemma gives

Cn2=|I|⋅|J|≤|I∩J|⋅|L|=Cn−1​Cn+1C_{n}^{2}=|I|\cdot|J|\leq|I\cap J|\cdot|L|=C_{n-1}C_{n+1}

finishing the proof. ∎

We now consider the Motzkin numbers. A Motzkin path of length nn is a lattice path PP which satisfies

  1. 1.

    PP starts at p0=(0,0)p_{0}=(0,0) and ends at pn=(n,0)p_{n}=(n,0),

  2. 2.

    PP uses steps UU, DD, and horizontal H=[1,0]H=[1,0] and never goes below the xx-axis.

Let

ℳn={P∣P is a Motzkin path of length n}{\cal M}_{n}=\{P\mid\text{$P$ is a Motzkin path of length $n$}\}

so that

|ℳn|=Mn,|{\cal M}_{n}|=M_{n},

the nnth Motzkin number. The set ℳn{\cal M}_{n} ordered by (4) is a distributive lattice as demonstrated in [FP05]. Showing that the Motzkin sequence is log-convex is much like the proof of the previous theorem, with II and JJ replaced by

I={P∈ℳn+1∣P=H​P′ for some translated Motzkin path P′ of length n},I=\{P\in{\cal M}_{n+1}\mid\text{$P=HP^{\prime}$ for some translated Motzkin path $P^{\prime}$ of length $n$}\},

and

J={P∈ℳn+1∣P=P′​H for some Motzkin path P′ of length n}.J=\{P\in{\cal M}_{n+1}\mid\text{$P=P^{\prime}H$ for some Motzkin path $P^{\prime}$ of length $n$}\}.

So, we leave the details to the reader. This result was proved algebraically by Aigner [Aig98]. A combinatorial proof for both Motzkin and the large Schröder numbers was given by Chen, Wang, and Zheng [CWZ21].

Theorem 2.2.

The sequence (Mn)n≥0(M_{n})_{n\geq 0} of Motzkin numbers is log-convex. ∎

Finally, we investigate the large Schröder numbers. A Schröder path of semilength nn is a lattice path PP satisfying

  1. 1.

    PP starts at p0=(0,0)p_{0}=(0,0) and ends at pn=(n,0)p_{n}=(n,0),

  2. 2.

    PP uses steps UU, DD, and twice horizontal T=[2,0]T=[2,0] and never goes below the xx-axis.

If we let

𝒮n={P∣P is a Schröder path of semilength n}{\cal S}_{n}=\{P\mid\text{$P$ is a Schr\"{o}der path of semilength $n$}\}

then

|𝒮n|=Sn,|{\cal S}_{n}|=S_{n},

the nnth large Schröder number. As usual, we order 𝒮n{\cal S}_{n} using (4). However, this poset is not covered by the general theorem of [FP05], although they remark that it can be shown that the poset is a lattice. It is, in fact, distributive.

Lemma 2.3.

The poset 𝒮n{\cal S}_{n} is a distributive lattice.

Proof.

We first wish to show the existence of meets and joins. Suppose K,L∈𝒮nK,L\in{\cal S}_{n}. We claim that there is K∧L∈𝒮nK\wedge L\in{\cal S}_{n} such that

A⁡(K∧L)=A⁡(K)∩A⁡(L).A(K\wedge L)=A(K)\cap A(L).

To see this, consider any Schröder path L:p0,p1,…,pnL:p_{0},p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}. Since LL starts at (0,0)(0,0) and uses steps U,H,TU,H,T it must be that the coordinates of each pip_{i} have the same parity. It follows that KK and LL can only intersect at points which are endpoints of steps in both paths and cannot cross in the middle of a step. From this, the assertion that A⁡(K)∩A⁡(L)A(K)\cap A(L) is the area under some Schröder path follows. Similarly, there is K∨LK\vee L defined by

A⁡(K∨L)=A⁡(K)∪A⁡(L).A(K\vee L)=A(K)\cup A(L).

It is now an easy matter to verify that K∧LK\wedge L and K∨LK\vee L are indeed greatest lower bounds and least upper bounds. And distributivity follows from the fact that intersection distributes over union. ∎

Using the ideals

I={P∈𝒮n+1∣P=T​P′ for some translated Schröder path P′ of semilength n},I=\{P\in{\cal S}_{n+1}\mid\text{$P=TP^{\prime}$ for some translated Schr\"{o}der path $P^{\prime}$ of semilength $n$}\},

and

J={P∈𝒮n+1∣P=P′​T for some Schröder path P′ of semilength n},J=\{P\in{\cal S}_{n+1}\mid\text{$P=P^{\prime}T$ for some Schr\"{o}der path $P^{\prime}$ of semilength $n$}\},

the next result follows in the way to which we have become accustomed.

Theorem 2.4.

The sequence (Sn)n≥0(S_{n})_{n\geq 0} of Schröder numbers is log-convex. ∎

3 Young’s lattice

In this section we collect various log-concavity and log-convexity results which can be proved using closed intervals in Young’s lattice, YY. Since YY is a distributive lattice, so is every closed interval and we need not check that part of the hypothesis of the Order Ideal Lemma. We start by establishing some standard definitions and notation, including

[n]={1,2,…,n}.[n]=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.

An integer partition is a weakly decreasing sequence λ=(λ1,λ2,…,λk)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{k}) of nonnegative integers called parts. Note that we allow zero as a part. The Young diagram of λ\lambda consists of left-justified rows of boxes or cells with λi\lambda_{i} boxes in row ii. We will use English notation for Young diagrams with the first row on top and make no distinction between a partition and its Young diagram. For example, the shape of λ=(5,3,1)\lambda=(5,3,1) is shown in the upper left in Figure 4. Young’s lattice, YY, is the set of all partitions with partial order λ⪯μ\lambda\preceq\mu if the Young diagram of λ\lambda is contained in that of μ\mu.

We first show how our proof of the log-convexity of the Catalan numbers can be viewed in this setting. Consider the interval

𝒞n=[∅,(n−1,n−2,…,0)]{\cal C}_{n}=[\emptyset,(n-1,n-2,\ldots,0)]

The southeast boundary of any λ∈𝒞n\lambda\in{\cal C}_{n} can be considered as a lattice path of length 2​n2n from the lower left corner to the upper right corner of (n−1,n−2,…,0)(n-1,n-2,\ldots,0) using the edges of squares as unit steps north or east. And the lattice path must stay above the line y=xy=x if its initial point is taken as (0,0)(0,0). Such paths are another of the standard ways of describing Dyck paths. So the proof of Theorem 2.1 could have been given in the language of partitions.

For our next result, if λ=(λ1,λ2,…,λk)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{k}) is a partition and n​0n0 is an integer then we define

λ+n=(λ1+n,λ2+n,…,λk+n).\lambda+n=(\lambda_{1}+n,\lambda_{2}+n,\ldots,\lambda_{k}+n). (5)
Theorem 3.1.

For any partition λ\lambda, the sequence (#⁡[λ,λ+n])n≥0(\ \#[\lambda,\lambda+n]\ )_{n\geq 0} is log-concave.

Proof.

Let In=[λ,λ+n]I_{n}=[\lambda,\lambda+n] and consider the following as subsets of In+1I_{n+1}:

I=[λ,λ+n]I=[\lambda,\lambda+n]

and

J=[λ+1,λ+n+1].J=[\lambda+1,\lambda+n+1].

As in the previous proof, II is an lower order ideal, JJ is an upper order ideal, and I=In≅JI=I_{n}\cong J. As expected, I∩J=[λ+1,λ+n]≅In−1I\cap J=[\lambda+1,\lambda+n]\cong I_{n-1}. So we are done by the Order Ideal Lemma. ∎

Note that even more generally, λ\lambda could be replaced by a skew partition in the previous result and the proof would go through without change. As an application, suppose that λ=(1k)\lambda=(1^{k}) where we us the notation imi^{m} to indicate that ii is repeated mm times Then the μ∈[λ,λ+n]\mu\in[\lambda,\lambda+n] are precisely the kk-element multisubsets of [n+1][n+1]. These are counted by (n+kk)\binom{n+k}{k} and so we immediately get the following specialization of Theorem 3.1.

Corollary 3.2.

For any k≥0k\geq 0, the sequence ((n+kk))n≥0\left(\ \binom{n+k}{k}\ \right)_{n\geq 0} is log-concave. ∎

4 Order polynomials

The order polynomial of a labeled poset was introduced by Stanley in his thesis [Sta71] and has since been shown to be a fundamental invariant. In this section we prove that the sequence of values of the order polynomial of any labeled poset is log-concave. This permits us to prove log-concavity of sequences formed by specializing the Schur function corresponding to any partition. The enriched order polynomials of Stembridge [Ste97] are also shown to give rise to log-concave sequences, again independent of the underlying poset. This gives rise to log-concave sequences of specializations of Schur QQ-functions. We begin, as usual, with the necessary definitions. Note that some of the inequalities have been reversed from Stanley’s original definitions, but this does not change the theory in any substantive way.

Let (P,⪯)(P,\preceq) be a poset on [p][p]. The reader should be sure to distinguish the use of ⪯\preceq for the partial order on PP and ≤\leq for the total order on the integers. A poset on [3][3] is displayed in Figure 2. A PP-partition with range [n][n] is a map f:P→[n]f:P\rightarrow[n] such that for all x≺yx\prec y we have

  1. 1.

    f⁡(x)≤f⁡(y)f(x)\leq f(y) (that is, ff is order preserving), and

  2. 2.

    if x>yx>y then f⁡(x)<f⁡(y)f(x)<f(y).

Define

𝒪P​(n)={f∣f is a P-partition with range n}.{\cal O}_{P}(n)=\{f\mid\text{$f$ is a $P$-partition with range $n$}\}.

Returning to the example poset in Figure 2 we have

𝒪P(n)={f:P→[n]∣f(2)<f(1) and f(2)≤f(3)}.{\cal O}_{P}(n)=\{f:P\rightarrow[n]\mid f(2)<f(1)\text{ and }f(2)\leq f(3)\}.

The order polynomial of PP is

ΩP​(n)=#​𝒪P​(n).\Omega_{P}(n)=\#{\cal O}_{P}(n).
Theorem 4.1 ([Sta71]).

For any PP on [p][p] we have ΩP​(n)\Omega_{P}(n) is a polynomial in nn. ∎

We now turn 𝒪p​(n){\cal O}_{p}(n) into a poset by ordering PP-partitions component-wise, that is,

f≤gf\leq g if and only if f⁡(x)≤g⁡(x)f(x)\leq g(x) for all x∈Px\in P.

Even though we are using ≤\leq for both the partial order on functions and the total order on integers, context should distinguish them. Continuing to use the poset in Figure 2, we have displayed the partial order on 𝒪P​(3){\cal O}_{P}(3) in Figure 3. Note that the values of the functions ff are displayed outside the circles containing the elements of PP itself. The following result was proved in the special case that PP is naturally labeled (that is, x≺yx\prec y implies x<yx<y) by Chan, Pak and Panova [CPP23], and in full generality by Brenti [Bre89, Theorem 7.6.5]

Theorem 4.2.

For any PP on [p][p], the sequence (ΩP​(n))n≥0(\Omega_{P}(n))_{n\geq 0} is log-concave.

Proof.

We first need to prove that 𝒪P​(n){\cal O}_{P}(n) is a distributive lattice. Given f,g∈𝒪P​(n)f,g\in{\cal O}_{P}(n) we define a new function f∧g:P→[n]f\wedge g:P\rightarrow[n] by taking component-wise minima

(f∧g)​(x)=min⁡{f⁡(x),g⁡(x)}(f\wedge g)(x)=\min\{f(x),g(x)\}

for all x∈Px\in P. This will clearly be a greatest lower bound provided that f∧gf\wedge g is a PP-partition. Checking the two axioms are similar, so we only do the second. So suppose that x⪯yx\preceq y and x>yx>y. Then f⁡(x)<f⁡(y)f(x)<f(y) and g⁡(x)<g⁡(y)g(x)<g(y). Without loss of generality we can assume that f⁡(y)≤g⁡(y)f(y)\leq g(y). So,

min⁡{f⁡(x),g⁡(x)}≤f⁡(x)<f⁡(y)=min⁡{f⁡(y),g⁡(y)}\min\{f(x),g(x)\}\leq f(x)<f(y)=\min\{f(y),g(y)\}

as desired.

Similarly, we define f∨gf\vee g by

(f∨g)​(x)=max⁡{f⁡(x),g⁡(x)}(f\vee g)(x)=\max\{f(x),g(x)\}

for all x∈Px\in P. The fact that this is a least upper bound is much like what was done for the meet. And the distributive law follows from the fact that maximum distributes over minimum.

To apply the Order Ideal Lemma, let

L=𝒪P​(n+1)L={\cal O}_{P}(n+1)

so that |L|=ΩP​(n+1)|L|=\Omega_{P}(n+1). Now define

I={f∈L∣f⁡(x)≤n​ for all ​x∈P}.I=\{f\in L\mid f(x)\leq n\text{ for all }x\in P\}.

Clearly II is a lower order ideal since we are applying an upper bound on ff. Furthermore, I=𝒪P​(n)I={\cal O}_{P}(n) so that |I|=Ωp​(n)|I|=\Omega_{p}(n). Also consider

J={f∈L∣f⁡(x)≥2​ for all ​x∈P}.J=\{f\in L\mid f(x)\geq 2\text{ for all }x\in P\}.

This is an upper order ideal and J≅𝒪P​(n)J\cong{\cal O}_{P}(n) where the isomorphism is obtained by subtracting one from each f⁡(x)f(x). It follows that |J|=ΩP​(n)|J|=\Omega_{P}(n). Similar considerations show that I∩J≅𝒪P​(n−1)I\cap J\cong{\cal O}_{P}(n-1) so that |I∩J|=ΩP​(n−1)|I\cap J|=\Omega_{P}(n-1). This completes the proof. ∎

We now use the well-known connection between order polynomials and Schur functions to derive an interesting special case of the previous theorem. If λ\lambda is an integer partition then a semistandard Young tableau (SSYT) of shape λ\lambda is a filling of the boxes of λ\lambda with positive integers such that rows weakly increase left-to-right and columns strictly increase top-to-bottom. The partition λ=(5,3,1)\lambda=(5,3,1) and a semistandard Young tableau TT of that shape are displayed in the first row of Figure 4. We let (i,j)(i,j) be the cell of λ\lambda in row ii and column jj where rows and columns are indexed as in a matrix. Given an SSYT of shape λ\lambda we denote by Ti,jT_{i,j} the element of TT in box (i,j)(i,j). In the tableau of Figure 4 we have T2,3=5T_{2,3}=5. Consider

SSYTλ={T∣T is an SSYT of shape λ}.\SSYT_{\lambda}=\{T\mid\text{$T$ is an SSYT of shape $\lambda$}\}.

Let 𝐱={x1,x2,…}{\bf x}=\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots\} be a set of variables indexed by the positive integers. The Schur function corresponding to λ\lambda is the generating function

sλ​(𝐱)=∑T∈SSYTλ∏(i,j)∈λxTi,j.s_{\lambda}({\bf x})=\sum_{T\in\SSYT_{\lambda}}\prod_{(i,j)\in\lambda}x_{T_{i,j}}.

The Schur functions are symmetric and form an important basis for the algebra of symmetric functions. For more information about them, see the texts of Sagan [Sag01] or Stanley [Sta24].

To make the connection with PP-partitions, we first turn λ=(λ1,λ2,…,λk)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{k}) into a poset component-wise, that is

(i,j)⪯(i′,j′)(i,j)\preceq(i^{\prime},j^{\prime}) if and only if i≤i′i\leq i^{\prime} and j≤j′j\leq j^{\prime}. (6)

We now make this a poset PλP_{\lambda} on the interval [|λ|][|\lambda|] where |λ|=∑lλl|\lambda|=\sum_{l}\lambda_{l} by labeling the last row of λ\lambda with 1,2,…,λk1,2,\ldots,\lambda_{k} left-to-right (viewing λ\lambda as its original Young diagram). Then labeling the penultimate row left-to-right with λk+1,λk+2,…,λk+λk−1\lambda_{k}+1,\lambda_{k}+2,\ldots,\lambda_{k}+\lambda_{k-1}, and so forth. This labeling is displayed in Figure 4 at the bottom left. It is easy to see that a PλP_{\lambda}-partition is the same as an SSYT of shape λ\lambda. The partition for the SSYT TT in Figure 4 is displayed directly below the tableau. It should now be clear that we have

sλ​(1n)=ΩPλ​(n)s_{\lambda}(1^{n})=\Omega_{P_{\lambda}}(n)

where 1n1^{n} indicates the specialization

xi=1x_{i}=1 for i≤ni\leq n and xi=0x_{i}=0 for i>ni>n.

As an immediate consequence of Theorem 4.2, we have the following result which is also implicit in Brenti’s work [Bre89, Theorems 5.2.3 and 7.6.5].

Corollary 4.3.

For any partition λ\lambda, the sequence (sλ​(1n))n≥0(s_{\lambda}(1^{n}))_{n\geq 0} is log-concave. ∎

We can also apply the Order Ideal Lemma to the enriched PP-partitions of Stembridge [Ste97]. We put an unusual total order on the nonzero integers, where we denote −n-n by n¯\overline{n},

1¯⊲1⊲2¯⊲2⊲3¯⊲3⊲…\overline{1}\triangleleft 1\triangleleft\overline{2}\triangleleft 2\triangleleft\overline{3}\triangleleft 3\triangleleft\ldots\ (7)

and also let

⟨n⟩={1¯,1,2¯,2,…,n¯,n}.\langle{n}\rangle=\{\overline{1},1,\overline{2},2,\ldots,\overline{n},n\}.

An enriched PP-partition with range ⟨n⟩\langle{n}\rangle is a map f:P→⟨n⟩f:P\rightarrow\langle{n}\rangle such that for all x≺yx\prec y we have

  1. (E1)

    f⁡(x)​⊴​f​(y)f(x)\trianglelefteq f(y),

  2. (E2)

    f⁡(x)=f⁡(y)>0f(x)=f(y)>0 implies x<yx<y, and

  3. (E3)

    f⁡(x)=f⁡(y)<0f(x)=f(y)<0 implies x>yx>y.

We now let

𝒪Pe​(n)={f∣f is an enriched P-partition with range ⟨n⟩}.{\cal O}_{P}^{e}(n)=\{f\mid\text{$f$ is an enriched $P$-partition with range $\langle{n}\rangle$}\}.

with corresponding enriched order polynomial

ΩPe​(n)=#​𝒪Pe​(n).\Omega_{P}^{e}(n)=\#{\cal O}_{P}^{e}(n).

As with the ordinary order polynomial, the enriched one is well named.

Theorem 4.4 ([Ste97]).

For any PP on [p][p] we have ΩPe​(n)\Omega_{P}^{e}(n) is a polynomial in nn. ∎

We now turn 𝒪Pe​(n){\cal O}_{P}^{e}(n) into a poset in exactly the same way as the ordinary case:

f≤gf\leq g if and only if f⁡(x)​⊴​g​(x)f(x)\trianglelefteq g(x) for all x∈Px\in P.

Figure 5 shows the partial order 𝒪Pe​(2){\cal O}_{P}^{e}(2) using our canonical poset PP in Figure 2. The proof of the next result is much like that of Theorem 4.2 and so is omitted.

Theorem 4.5.

For any PP on [p][p], the sequence (ΩPe​(n))n≥0(\Omega_{P}^{e}(n))_{n\geq 0} is log-concave. ∎

The appropriate tableaux for the enriched setting arise from shifted shapes. An integer partition λ=(λ1,λ2,…,λk)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{k}) is strict if λ1>λ2>…>λk\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}>\ldots>\lambda_{k}. A strict partition has an associated shifted Young diagram obtained from the ordinary Young diagram by shifting the iith row i−1i-1 boxes to the right for i∈[k]i\in[k]. The shifted shape of λ=(6,5,3,2)\lambda=(6,5,3,2) is shown on the left in Figure 6. A semistandard Young tableau of shifted shape λ\lambda is a filling TT of the cells of λ\lambda with nonzero integers such that the following are satisfied.

  1. (T1)

    The rows and columns of TT are weakly increasing with respect to the total order 7.

  2. (T2)

    For each m>0m>0 there is at most one m¯\overline{m} in each row and at most one mm in each column.

We let

SSYTSλ={T∣T is a semistandard Young tableau of shifted shape λ}\SSYTS_{\lambda}=\{T\mid\text{$T$ is a semistandard Young tableau of shifted shape $\lambda$}\}

with generating function

Qλ​(𝐱)=∑SSYTSλ∏(i,j)∈λx|Ti,j|Q_{\lambda}({\bf x})=\sum_{\SSYTS_{\lambda}}\prod_{(i,j)\in\lambda}x_{|T_{i,j}|}

which is called a Schur QQ-function. These functions play a role in the projective representation theory of the symmetric group analogous to sλ​(𝐱)s_{\lambda}({\bf x}) for ordinary representations.

The partial order on shifted shape is just the restriction of (6) to those cells in the shifted Young diagram. And the labeling to get a corresponding partition PλeP_{\lambda}^{e} on [|λ|][|\lambda|] is exactly the same as in the unshifted case, starting with the bottom row and working up. Now axiom (E1) for enriched PP-partitions implies condition (T1) for semistandard shifted Young tableaux. And axioms (E2) and (E3) translate into condition (T2). Thus

Qλ​(1n)=ΩPλe​(n)Q_{\lambda}(1^{n})=\Omega_{P_{\lambda}^{e}}(n)

and the next result is a special case of Theorem 4.4.

Corollary 4.6.

For any strict partition λ\lambda, the sequence (Qλ​(1n))n≥0(Q_{\lambda}(1^{n}))_{n\geq 0} is log-concave. ∎

5 Generalized Lucas sequences

A sequence (ln)n≥0(l_{n})_{n\geq 0} of real numbers is a generalized Lucas sequence if it satisfies the recursion

ln=ln−1+ln−2l_{n}=l_{n-1}+l_{n-2} (8)

for n≥2n\geq 2. These sequences were originally studied by Lucas [Luc78a, Luc78b, Luc78c]. Both the sequences themselves and their qq-analogues have many wonderful combinatorial properties, see [BP09, BCMS20, SS10, ST20]. Of course, the two most famous examples of such sequences are the Fibonacci numbers, (Fn)n≥0(F_{n})_{n\geq 0}, and (ordinary) Lucas numbers, (Ln)n≥0(L_{n})_{n\geq 0}, with initial conditions F0=F1=1F_{0}=F_{1}=1 and L0=2L_{0}=2, L1=1L_{1}=1, respectively.

In this section we will study positive Lucas sequences which are generalized Lucas sequences with l0,l1>0l_{0},l_{1}>0. In order to state our result precisely, call a sequence (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} log-concave at index nn if

an2≥an−1​an+1.a_{n}^{2}\geq a_{n-1}a_{n+1}.

Note that this definition says nothing about indices other than nn. Similarly define log-convexity at index nn. We will show that any positive Lucas sequence, suitably reindexed, alternates between being log-concave at odd indices and log-convex at even ones.

It will be convenient in our approach to restrict the initial values even further. But we wish to first show that this restriction will be, in some sense, without loss of generality. To do this, we extend a generalized Lucas sequence to negative indices by insisting that the recurrence relation (8) continue to hold for n<0n<0 to give an extended Lucas sequence (ln)n∈ℤ(l_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{Z}}}. Call two extended Lucas sequences (ln)n∈ℤ(l_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{Z}}} and (ln′)n∈ℤ(l^{\prime}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{Z}}} shift equivalent if there is k∈ℤk\in{\mathbb{Z}} such that

ln=ln+k′l_{n}=l^{\prime}_{n+k}

for all n∈ℤn\in{\mathbb{Z}}.

Proposition 5.1.

Suppose that (ln)n≥0(l_{n})_{n\geq 0} is a positive Lucas sequence. Then its extension is shift equivalent to an extended Lucas sequence (ln′)n∈ℤ(l^{\prime}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{Z}}} such that

0<2​l0′≤l1′.0<2l^{\prime}_{0}\leq l^{\prime}_{1}.
Proof.

Consider the reverse subsequence l1,l0,l−1,…l_{1},l_{0},l_{-1},\ldots of the given Lucas sequence. Suppose first that this sequence contains a weak ascent lj≤lj−1l_{j}\leq l_{j-1} where lj,lj−1>0l_{j},l_{j-1}>0. But then

lj+1=lj+lj−1≥2​lj>0,l_{j+1}=l_{j}+l_{j-1}\geq 2l_{j}>0,

as desired.

Now suppose this sequence contains a weak ascent with lj=0l_{j}=0, Then lj−1>0l_{j-1}>0 since otherwise all entries in the original Lucas sequence are nonpositive. But now

lj+2=lj+1+lj=lj+1,l_{j+2}=l_{j+1}+l_{j}=l_{j+1},

where

lj+1=lj+lj−1=lj−1>0.l_{j+1}=l_{j}+l_{j-1}=l_{j-1}>0.

So

lj+3=lj+2+lj+1=2​lj+2>0,l_{j+3}=l_{j+2}+l_{j+1}=2l_{j+2}>0,

again giving the correct conclusion.

If there are no such weak ascents, then the sequence is strictly decreasing and so must eventually become negative. Let mm be the index of minimum absolute value such that lm<0l_{m}<0. It follows that lm+1≥0l_{m+1}\geq 0 and

0≤lm+2=lm+1+lm≤lm+1.0\leq l_{m+2}=l_{m+1}+l_{m}\leq l_{m+1}.

But this is a weak ascent which is a contradiction. ∎

We will now introduce the posets whose lattices of order ideals will permit us to study the behaviour of positive Lucas sequences (ln)n≥0(l_{n})_{n\geq 0}. Say that such a sequence is well-indexed if

0<2​l0≤l1.0<2l_{0}\leq l_{1}.

Note that, by the previous proposition, every positive Lucas sequence is shift equivalent to a well-indexed one. To simplify notation, we will relabel

r:=l0​ and ​s:=l1r:=l_{0}\text{ and }s:=l_{1} (9)

Define a poset Ln​(r,s)L_{n}(r,s) to have elements x1,…,xs−1x_{1},\ldots,x_{s-1} and y2,…,yny_{2},\ldots,y_{n} and order relation ⪯\preceq subject to the covers

  1. 1.

    x1≺x2≺…≺xs−1x_{1}\prec x_{2}\prec\ldots\prec x_{s-1},

  2. 2.

    y2≺y3≻y4≺y5≻…y_{2}\prec y_{3}\succ y_{4}\prec y_{5}\succ\ldots, and

  3. 3.

    y2≺xry_{2}\prec x_{r}.

So the xix_{i} form a chain Cs−1C_{s-1} and the yjy_{j} form what we will call an alternating poset An−1A_{n-1}. For example, Figure 7 shows the poset L5​(3,7)L_{5}(3,7).

Let J⁡(P)J(P) denote the set of lower order ideals of a finite poset PP. It is a fundamental result that J⁡(P)J(P) is a distributive lattice for any PP. This construction will permit us to prove the following theorem. Note that since the Fibonacci sequence satisfies

Fn2=Fn−1​Fn+1+(−1)n−1,F_{n}^{2}=F_{n-1}F_{n+1}+(-1)^{n-1},

one sees immediately that the result is true in this case.

Theorem 5.2.

A well-indexed Lucas sequence (ln)n≥0(l_{n})_{n\geq 0} is log-concave at odd indices and log-convex at even ones.

Proof.

We continue to use the notation in (9). We first verify log-concavity at index n=1n=1 since our approach with ideals will only start to work when n≥2n\geq 2. Since r≤s/2r\leq s/2 we have

l0​l2=r⁡(r+s)≤s/2​(3​s/2)<s2=l12.l_{0}l_{2}=r(r+s)\leq s/2(3s/2)<s^{2}=l_{1}^{2}.

For ease of notation, let Ln=Ln​(r,s)L_{n}=L_{n}(r,s). We will show by induction that

#​J​(Ln)=ln\#J(L_{n})=l_{n} (10)

for n≥1n\geq 1. When n=1n=1 we have that L1L_{1} is a chain with s−1s-1 elements so that #​J​(L1)=s=l1\#J(L_{1})=s=l_{1}. Poset L2L_{2} is obtained from L1L_{1} by placing y2y_{2} under the rrth smallest element of the chain. So, counting the ideals with 0,1,2,…0,1,2,\ldots elements we get

#​J​(L2)=1+2+⋯+2⏞r−1+1+⋯+1⏞s−r+1=r+s=l2.\#J(L_{2})=1+\overbrace{2+\cdots+2}^{r-1}+\overbrace{1+\cdots+1}^{s-r+1}=r+s=l_{2}.

The induction step has two cases depending on whether nn is odd or even. But they are similar so we will only do the former. In this case we have yn−1≺yny_{n-1}\prec y_{n}. Every ideal I∈J⁡(Ln)I\in J(L_{n}) either contains yny_{n} or not. It follows that if yn∉Iy_{n}\not\in I then I∈J⁡(Ln−1)I\in J(L_{n-1}). On the other hand, if yn∈Iy_{n}\in I then this forces yn−1∈Iy_{n-1}\in I and I−{yn−1,yn}∈J⁡(Ln−2)I-\{y_{n-1},y_{n}\}\in J(L_{n-2}). From these observations and induction

#​J​(Ln)=#​J​(Ln−1)+#​J​(Ln−2)=ln−1+ln−2=ln\#J(L_{n})=\#J(L_{n-1})+\#J(L_{n-2})=l_{n-1}+l_{n-2}=l_{n}

which completes the proof of the claim.

We now construct the ideals ℐn,𝒥n⊆J⁡(Ln+1){\cal I}_{n},{\cal J}_{n}\subseteq J(L_{n+1}) needed to prove the theorem. Given a set of constraints SS on ideals II we will use the notation

Jn+1​(S)={I∈J⁡(Ln+1)∣I satisfies S}.J_{n+1}(S)=\{I\in J(L_{n+1})\mid\text{$I$ satisfies $S$}\}.

Define

ℐn={Jn+1​(yn+1∈I)if n is odd,Jn+1​(yn+1∉I)if n is even.{\cal I}_{n}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}J_{n+1}(y_{n+1}\in I)&\mbox{if $n$ is odd,}\\ J_{n+1}(y_{n+1}\not\in I)&\mbox{if $n$ is even.}\end{array}\right.

Then

#​ℐn=ln.\#{\cal I}_{n}=l_{n}. (11)

In fact we have an isomorphism ℐn≅J⁡(Ln){\cal I}_{n}\cong J(L_{n}) given by the identity map on individual elements when nn is even, and by removal of yn+1y_{n+1} when nn is odd. So the claim follows from (10). Note that the ideals in ℐn{\cal I}_{n} form either an upper or lower order ideal in J⁡(Ln+1)J(L_{n+1}) depending on whether nn is odd or even, respectively.

Now let

𝒥n=Jn+1​(xr∉I)∪Jn+1​(xs−r∉I​ and ​yn+1∉I).{\cal J}_{n}=J_{n+1}(x_{r}\not\in I)\hskip 3.0pt\cup\hskip 3.0ptJ_{n+1}(x_{s-r}\not\in I\text{ and }y_{n+1}\not\in I).

Note that 𝒥n{\cal J}_{n} is a lower order ideal in J⁡(Ln+1)J(L_{n+1}) regardless of the parity of nn. We wish to show

#​𝒥n=ln.\#{\cal J}_{n}=l_{n}. (12)

In view of (11), it suffices to show that the set differences ℐn∖𝒥n{\cal I}_{n}\setminus{\cal J}_{n} and 𝒥n∖ℐn{\cal J}_{n}\setminus{\cal I}_{n} have the same cardinality. Again, we merely provide details when nn is even. Now

ℐn∖𝒥n=Jn+1​(xr∈I, and xs−r∈I, and yn+1∉I).{\cal I}_{n}\setminus{\cal J}_{n}=J_{n+1}(\text{$x_{r}\in I$, and $x_{s-r}\in I$, and $y_{n+1}\not\in I$}).

But r≤s−rr\leq s-r so that xr≤xs−rx_{r}\leq x_{s-r} in Ln+1L_{n+1}. This makes the condition xr∈Ix_{r}\in I redundant and

ℐn∖𝒥n=Jn+1​(xs−r∈I, and yn+1∉I).{\cal I}_{n}\setminus{\cal J}_{n}=J_{n+1}(\text{$x_{s-r}\in I$, and $y_{n+1}\not\in I$}).

Note that xs−rx_{s-r} is greater than y2y_{2} and all the xix_{i} below it. So those elements are forced to be in any ideal II we are considering. But then II must be constructed by adding to these elements some ideal of the chain xs−r+1,…,xs−1x_{s-r+1},\ldots,x_{s-1} and, because nn is even, an ideal of the subposet of Ln+1L_{n+1} induced on y3,…,yny_{3},\ldots,y_{n}. It follows that we have a product poset

ℐn∖𝒥n≅J⁡(Cr−1)×J⁡(An−2).{\cal I}_{n}\setminus{\cal J}_{n}\cong J(C_{r-1})\times J(A_{n-2}). (13)

Now directly from the definitions we have

𝒥n∖ℐn=Jn+1​(xr∉I, and yn+1∈I).{\cal J}_{n}\setminus{\cal I}_{n}=J_{n+1}(\text{$x_{r}\not\in I$, and $y_{n+1}\in I$}).

Since xr∉Ix_{r}\not\in I, any ideal in the difference breaks into two pieces. One is an ideal in the chain x1,…,xr−1x_{1},\ldots,x_{r-1} and the other an ideal of the alternating poset on y2,…,yn+1y_{2},\ldots,y_{n+1} which contains yn+1y_{n+1}. Since by parity, yn+1≻yny_{n+1}\succ y_{n}, we must also have yn∈Iy_{n}\in I and so this part of II is determined as an ideal in the alternating poset on y2,…,yn−1y_{2},\ldots,y_{n-1}. Comparing this with (13) shows that #​ℐn∖𝒥n=#​𝒥n∖ℐn\#{\cal I}_{n}\setminus{\cal J}_{n}=\#{\cal J}_{n}\setminus{\cal I}_{n}.

There remains to calculate #⁡(ℐn∩𝒥n)\#({\cal I}_{n}\cap{\cal J}_{n}). But directly from the definitions we see that the identity map on elements gives an isomorphism ℐn∩𝒥n≅𝒥n−1{\cal I}_{n}\cap{\cal J}_{n}\cong{\cal J}_{n-1}. So by (12) we have

#⁡(ℐn∩𝒥n)=ln−1\#({\cal I}_{n}\cap{\cal J}_{n})=l_{n-1}

as desired. ∎

6 Permutations

We now prove various log-concavity and log-convexity results concerning subsets of the symmetric group 𝔖n{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} of permutations of [n][n]. Sequences of evaluations of descent and peak polynomials will be shown to be log-concave. We will also use pattern avoidance to give a third proof of the log-convexity of the Catalan numbers. In addition to the Order Ideal Lemma, one of our main tools will be the recently-defined middle order distributive lattice on 𝔖n{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}.

There are two standard partial orders on 𝔖n{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}: the weak and strong Bruhat orders. Recently, Bouvel, Ferrari and Tenner [BFT24] defined a partial order which they call the middle order because it refines the weak order and is refined by the strong. This order has the advantage of being a distributive lattice and is built using inversions. Given π=π1​π2​…​πn∈𝔖n\pi=\pi_{1}\pi_{2}\ldots\pi_{n}\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} in one-line notation, its set of inversion (values) is

Inv⁡π={(πi,πj)∣i<j​ and ​πi>πj}.\Inv\pi=\{(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})\mid i<j\text{ and }\pi_{i}>\pi_{j}\}.

We also say that πi\pi_{i} is an inversion top if (πi,πj)∈Inv⁡π(\pi_{i},\pi_{j})\in\Inv\pi for some πj\pi_{j}. For example, if

π=415632\pi=415632 (14)

then

Inv⁡415632={(4,1),(4,2),(4,3),(5,2),(5,3),(6,2),(6,3),(3,2)}\Inv 415632=\{(4,1),\ (4,2),\ (4,3),\ (5,2),\ (5,3),\ (6,2),\ (6,3),\ (3,2)\}

so 44 is an inversion top in 33 inversions, 55 and 66 are inversion tops in 22 inversions each, and 33 is an inversion top in one inversion. Clearly ii can be an inversion top in anywhere from 00 to i−1i-1 inversions. The inversion table of π\pi is

ι⁡(π)=(ι1,ι2,…,ιn)\iota(\pi)=(\iota_{1},\iota_{2},\ldots,\iota_{n})

where

ιi= # of inversions in which i is an inversion top.\iota_{i}=\text{ \# of inversions in which $i$ is an inversion top}.

Returning to our example

ι⁡(π)=(0,0,1,3,2,2).\iota(\pi)=(0,0,1,3,2,2).

Let

ℐn={ι=(ι1,ι2,…,ιn)∣0≤ιi<i​ for all ​i∈[n]}.{\cal I}_{n}=\{\iota=(\iota_{1},\iota_{2},\ldots,\iota_{n})\mid 0\leq\iota_{i}<i\text{ for all }i\in[n]\}. (15)

It is well-known that there is a bijection 𝔖n→ℐn{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}\rightarrow{\cal I}_{n} given by π↦ι⁡(π)\pi\mapsto\iota(\pi).

We can now use the bijection just given to define the middle order (𝔖n,⪯)({\mathfrak{S}}_{n},\preceq) by

π⪯σ​ if and only if ​ι​(π)≤ι⁡(σ)\pi\preceq\sigma\text{ if and only if }\iota(\pi)\leq\iota(\sigma)

where the order on inversion tables is component-wise. Because of (15) we have that the middle order is isomorphic to a product of chains

𝔖n≅[0,0]×[0,1]×⋯×[0,n−1]{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}\cong[0,0]\times[0,1]\times\cdots\times[0,n-1]

where [0,i]={0,1,…,i}[0,i]=\{0,1,\ldots,i\} with the usual total order on the integers. It follows that this order is a distributive lattice. In Figure 8 we display this order both on the permutations in 𝔖3{\mathfrak{S}}_{3} on the left, as well as on their corresponding inversion tables on the right. It will sometimes be convenient to work directly with (ℐn,≤)({\cal I}_{n},\leq) rather than (𝔖n,≺)({\mathfrak{S}}_{n},\prec). We begin by showing that the sequence of factorials n!=#​𝔖nn!=\#{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} is log-convex. Of course, this can be proved by simple arithmetic. But our proof will serve as a model for later, more complicated ones, using the middle order.

Theorem 6.1.

The sequence (n!)n≥0(n!)_{n\geq 0} is log-convex

Proof.

Consider the two lower order ideals of ℐn+1{\cal I}_{n+1} given by

I={ι∈ℐn+1∣ιn+1=0}I=\{\iota\in{\cal I}_{n+1}\mid\iota_{n+1}=0\}

and

J={ι∈ℐn+1∣0≤ιi<i−1​ for all ​2≤i≤n+1}.J=\{\iota\in{\cal I}_{n+1}\mid 0\leq\iota_{i}<i-1\text{ for all }2\leq i\leq n+1\}.

Now I≅ℐn≅JI\cong{\cal I}_{n}\cong J where the first, respectively second, isomorphism is obtained by removing ιn+1\iota_{n+1}, respectively ι1\iota_{1}. Similarly I∩J≅ℐn−1I\cap J\cong{\cal I}_{n-1} and the Order Ideal Lemma once again finishes the demonstration. ∎

6.1 Descent polynomials

We now prove that sequences of evaluations of descent polynomials are log-concave. After this paper was published, it was discovered that therre was an error in the proof in that the intersection of the two proposed ideals did not have the correct cardinality. This was corrected in a later corrigendum, and that is the proof which will be presented here. The descent set of π∈𝔖n\pi\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} is

Des⁡π={i∣πi>πi+1}.\Des\pi=\{i\mid\pi_{i}>\pi_{i+1}\}.

Note that, unlike the inversion set, we are using the positions of the descents. If π\pi is as in (14) then

Des⁡415632={1,4,5}\Des 415632=\{1,4,5\} (16)

Let SS be any finite set of positive integers and consider

Dn​(S)={π∈𝔖n∣Des⁡π=S}D_{n}(S)=\{\pi\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}\mid\Des\pi=S\}

as well as

dn​(S)=#​Dn​(S)d_{n}(S)=\#D_{n}(S)

where the latter is called the descent polynomial corresponding to SS. For more information about descent polynomials see [DLHI+19, O20, GG21, Ben21, Ray23, JM23]. The following is a classic result of MacMahon [Mac04].

Theorem 6.2 ([Mac04]).

For any set SS and all n>max⁡Sn>\max S we have that dn​(S)d_{n}(S) is a polynomial in nn. ∎

In order to prove that (dn​(S))n≥0(d_{n}(S))_{n\geq 0} is always log-concave we will need a variant of the middle order which considers positions rather than values. The positional inversion table of π∈𝔖n\pi\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} is

κ⁡(π)=(κ1,κ2,…,κn)\kappa(\pi)=(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2},\ldots,\kappa_{n})

where

κi=#⁡{j>i∣πj<πi}.\kappa_{i}=\#\{j>i\mid\pi_{j}<\pi_{i}\}.

In other words, κi\kappa_{i} is the number of inversions with πi\pi_{i} as inversion top. Continuing with our example permutation

κ⁡(415632)=(3,0,2,2,1,0).\kappa(415632)=(3,0,2,2,1,0). (17)

Clearly 0≤κi≤n−i0\leq\kappa_{i}\leq n-i for all i∈[n]i\in[n]. Consider

𝒦n={κ=(κ1,κ2,…,κn)∣0≤κi≤n−i​ for all ​i∈[n]}.{\cal K}_{n}=\{\kappa=(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2},\ldots,\kappa_{n})\mid 0\leq\kappa_{i}\leq n-i\text{ for all }i\in[n]\}.

The bijection 𝒦n→𝔖n{\cal K}_{n}\rightarrow{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} given by κ↦π\kappa\mapsto\pi where κ⁡(π)=κ\kappa(\pi)=\kappa will be useful to us, so we describe it explicitly. Assuming that π1,…,πi−1\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{i-1} have been constructed, we let

πi= the (vi+1)st smallest element of [n]∖{π1,…,πi−1}.\pi_{i}=\text{ the $(v_{i}+1)$st smallest element of $[n]\setminus\{\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{i-1}$\lx@text@rbrace}. (18)

By way of illustration, suppose κ\kappa is as given in (17). Since κ1=3\kappa_{1}=3 we let π1\pi_{1} be the (3+1)(3+1)st smallest element of [6][6], that is π1=4\pi_{1}=4. Now κ2=0\kappa_{2}=0 so π2\pi_{2} will be the smallest element of [6]∖{4}[6]\setminus\{4\} so that π2=1\pi_{2}=1. Next κ3=2\kappa_{3}=2 so we pick the third smallest element of [6]∖{1,4}[6]\setminus\{1,4\} which gives π3=5\pi_{3}=5. Continuing in this way, we get π=415632\pi=415632 which agrees with the permutation which started this example.

We now define the κ\kappa-middle order (𝔖n,⊴)({\mathfrak{S}}_{n},\trianglelefteq) by

π​⊴​σ​ if and only if ​κ​(π)≤κ⁡(σ)\pi\trianglelefteq\sigma\text{ if and only if }\kappa(\pi)\leq\kappa(\sigma)

component-wise. In this partial order we have

𝔖n≅[0,n−1]×[0,n−2]×⋯×[0,0]{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}\cong[0,n-1]\times[0,n-2]\times\cdots\times[0,0]

so that, again, we have a distributive lattice. And, as with middle order, sometimes we will choose to work directly with 𝒦n{\cal K}_{n} rather than 𝔖n{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}. To do this, we need to be able to read off Des⁡π\Des\pi from κ⁡(π)\kappa(\pi) which turns out to be easy to do (and is one of the reasons for using κ\kappa rather than ι\iota). Define the descent set of κ∈𝒦n\kappa\in{\cal K}_{n} to be

Des⁡κ={i∣κi>κi+1}.\Des\kappa=\{i\mid\kappa_{i}>\kappa_{i+1}\}.

Note that we do not include ii in the descent set if κi=κi+1\kappa_{i}=\kappa_{i+1}. If κ\kappa is as in (17) then

Des⁡κ={1,4,5}.\Des\kappa=\{1,4,5\}.

Note that this is the same descent set as in (16). This is not an accident.

Lemma 6.3.

For any π∈𝔖n\pi\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} we have

Des⁡κ⁡(π)=Des⁡π.\Des\kappa(\pi)=\Des\pi.
Proof.

Say π=π1​π2​…​πn\pi=\pi_{1}\pi_{2}\ldots\pi_{n} and κ⁡(π)=(κ1,κ2,…,κn)\kappa(\pi)=(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2},\ldots,\kappa_{n}). Suppose first that i∈Des⁡κ⁡(π)i\in\Des\kappa(\pi) so that κi>κi+1\kappa_{i}>\kappa_{i+1}. From (18) we have that πi\pi_{i} is the (κi+1)(\kappa_{i}+1)st smallest element of a set SS and πi+1\pi_{i+1} is the (κi+1+1)(\kappa_{i+1}+1)st smallest in S∖{πi}S\setminus\{\pi_{i}\}. But since κi+1<κi\kappa_{i+1}<\kappa_{i} we also have that πi+1\pi_{i+1} is the (κi+1+1)(\kappa_{i+1}+1)st smallest in SS itself. Using the inequality κi+1<κi\kappa_{i+1}<\kappa_{i} again shows that πi+1<πi\pi_{i+1}<\pi_{i} so that i∈Des⁡πi\in\Des\pi. By a similar argument, if i∉Des⁡κ⁡(π)i\not\in\Des\kappa(\pi) then i∉Des⁡πi\not\in\Des\pi which completes the proof. ∎

We now define a partial order (Dn​(S),⊴)(D_{n}(S),\trianglelefteq) by restricting the κ\kappa-middle order on 𝔖n{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} to Dn​(S)D_{n}(S). We need to show that we still have a distributive lattice. In fact, we will show that Dn​(S)D_{n}(S) is a sublattice of 𝔖n{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} under ⊴\trianglelefteq. To do so, it will be convenient to extend the minimum and maximum functions to two integer vectors κ=(κ1,…,κn)\kappa=(\kappa_{1},\ldots,\kappa_{n}) and χ=(χ1,…,χn)\chi=(\chi_{1},\ldots,\chi_{n}) component-wise so that

min⁡{κ,χ}=(min⁡{κ1,χ1},…,min⁡{κn,χn})\min\{\kappa,\chi\}=(\min\{\kappa_{1},\chi_{1}\},\ldots,\min\{\kappa_{n},\chi_{n}\}) (19)

and

max⁡{κ,χ}=(max⁡{κ1,χ1},…,max⁡{κn,χn}).\max\{\kappa,\chi\}=(\max\{\kappa_{1},\chi_{1}\},\ldots,\max\{\kappa_{n},\chi_{n}\}). (20)
Lemma 6.4.

If κ,χ∈𝒦n\kappa,\chi\in{\cal K}_{n} have Des⁡κ=S=Des⁡χ\Des\kappa=S=\Des\chi then

Des⁡(min⁡{κ,χ})=S=Des⁡(max⁡{κ,χ}).\Des(\min\{\kappa,\chi\})=S=\Des(\max\{\kappa,\chi\}).
Proof.

We will prove the min\min statement as the max\max one is similar. It suffices to show that if i∈Si\in S then i∈Des⁡(min⁡{κ,χ})i\in\Des(\min\{\kappa,\chi\}) and similarly for i∉Si\not\in S.

If i∈Si\in S then we have κi>κi+1\kappa_{i}>\kappa_{i+1} and χi>χi+1\chi_{i}>\chi_{i+1} Without loss of generality, we can assume κi≤χi\kappa_{i}\leq\chi_{i} so that min⁡{κi,χi}=κi\min\{\kappa_{i},\chi_{i}\}=\kappa_{i}. Thus

min⁡{κi+1,χi+1}≤κi+1<κi=min⁡{κi,χi}\min\{\kappa_{i+1},\chi_{i+1}\}\leq\kappa_{i+1}<\kappa_{i}=\min\{\kappa_{i},\chi_{i}\}

which implies that i∈Des⁡(min⁡{κ,χ})i\in\Des(\min\{\kappa,\chi\}). The analogous argument when i∉Si\not\in S is left to the reader. ∎

We now have everything in place to show that Dn​(S)D_{n}(S) is a distributive lattice.

Lemma 6.5.

For any SS the κ\kappa-middle order on Dn​(S)D_{n}(S) forms a distributive lattice.

Proof.

Consider π,σ∈Dn​(S)\pi,\sigma\in D_{n}(S). Define the meet and join operations by letting π∧σ\pi\wedge\sigma and π∨σ\pi\vee\sigma be the unique permutations such that

κ⁡(π∧σ)=min⁡{κ⁡(π),κ⁡(σ)}\kappa(\pi\wedge\sigma)=\min\{\kappa(\pi),\kappa(\sigma)\}

and

κ⁡(π∨σ)=max⁡{κ⁡(π),κ⁡(σ)}.\kappa(\pi\vee\sigma)=\max\{\kappa(\pi),\kappa(\sigma)\}.

We must first check that the meet and join are still in Dn​(S)D_{n}(S), that is, have descent set SS. But Des⁡π=S=Des⁡σ\Des\pi=S=\Des\sigma so that, by the previous lemma, Des⁡κ⁡(π)=S=Des⁡κ⁡(σ)\Des\kappa(\pi)=S=\Des\kappa(\sigma). Now using both the previous lemmas

Des⁡π∧σ=Des⁡κ⁡(π∧σ)=Des⁡(min⁡{κ⁡(π),κ⁡(σ)})=S.\Des\pi\wedge\sigma=\Des\kappa(\pi\wedge\sigma)=\Des(\min\{\kappa(\pi),\kappa(\sigma)\})=S.

The join case is similar.

We now show that the definition of meet actually gives a greatest lower bound, leaving the least upper bound property as an exercise for the reader. First of all we note that κ⁡(π∧σ)=min⁡{κ⁡(π),κ⁡(σ)}≤κ⁡(π),κ⁡(σ)\kappa(\pi\wedge\sigma)=\min\{\kappa(\pi),\kappa(\sigma)\}\leq\kappa(\pi),\kappa(\sigma) component-wise so that π∧σ≤π,σ\pi\wedge\sigma\leq\pi,\sigma. Now suppose that τ≤π,σ\tau\leq\pi,\sigma. By definition of the κ\kappa-middle order we have κ⁡(τ)≤κ⁡(π),κ⁡(σ)\kappa(\tau)\leq\kappa(\pi),\kappa(\sigma) component-wise. But then κ⁡(τ)≤min⁡{κ⁡(π),κ⁡(σ)}\kappa(\tau)\leq\min\{\kappa(\pi),\kappa(\sigma)\} so that τ≤π∧σ\tau\leq\pi\wedge\sigma.

That meet distributes over join follows easily from the fact that min distributes over max and so the proof is omitted. ∎

Now define

𝒦n​(S)={κ∈𝒦n∣Des⁡κ=S}{\cal K}_{n}(S)=\{\kappa\in{\cal K}_{n}\mid\Des\kappa=S\}

and partially order this set component-wise. From what we have shown, 𝒦n​(S)≅Dn​(S){\cal K}_{n}(S)\cong D_{n}(S) and so is a distributive lattice of size dn​(S)d_{n}(S). We will need the following facts about 𝒦n​(S){\cal K}_{n}(S).

Lemma 6.6.

Suppose S≠∅S\neq\emptyset and let m=max⁡Sm=\max S. Suppose κ=(κ1,…,κn)∈𝒦n​(S)\kappa=(\kappa_{1},\ldots,\kappa_{n})\in{\cal K}_{n}(S).

  1. (a)

    We have κm≥1\kappa_{m}\geq 1.

  2. (b)

    We have κi=0\kappa_{i}=0 for i>mi>m.

Proof.

(a) Since m∈S=Des⁡κm\in S=\Des\kappa we must have κm>κm+1≥0\kappa_{m}>\kappa_{m+1}\geq 0. But this implies κm≥1\kappa_{m}\geq 1.

(b) Suppose, towards a contradiction, that κi>0\kappa_{i}>0 for some i>mi>m. By definition of 𝒦n{\cal K}_{n} we have κn=0\kappa_{n}=0. So there must be an index j≥i>mj\geq i>m such that κj>0\kappa_{j}>0 and κj+1=0\kappa_{j+1}=0. But then j∈Des⁡κj\in\Des\kappa, contradicting the maximality of mm. ∎

We can now prove the main result of this subsection.

Theorem 6.7.

For any SS, the sequence (dn​(S))n≥0(d_{n}(S))_{n\geq 0} is log-concave.

Proof.

The result is easy if S=∅S=\emptyset, so we assume SS is nonempty. Keeping the notation of the previous lemma, we see that if κ∈𝒦n​(S)\kappa\in{\cal K}_{n}(S) then in fact

κ∈[0,n−1]×[0,n−2]×⋯×[0,n−m+1]×[1,n−m]×[0,0]n−m\kappa\in[0,n-1]\times[0,n-2]\times\cdots\times[0,n-m+1]\times[1,n-m]\times[0,0]^{n-m}

where the superscript denotes the (n−m)(n-m)-fold product.

Now consider the lattice 𝒦n+1​(S){\cal K}_{n+1}(S) so that |𝒦n+1​(S)|=dn+1​(S)|{\cal K}_{n+1}(S)|=d_{n+1}(S). Inside this lattice, define the set

I=𝒦n​(S)×[0,0].I={\cal K}_{n}(S)\times[0,0].

Clearly II is a lower order ideal with I≅Dn​(S)I\cong D_{n}(S) so that |I|=dn​(S)|I|=d_{n}(S). Also construct

J=𝒦n+1(S)∩([1,n]×[1,n−1]×⋯×[1,n−m+2]×[2,n−m+1]×[0,0]n−m+1).J={\cal K}_{n+1}(S)\cap([1,n]\times[1,n-1]\times\cdots\times[1,n-m+2]\times[2,n-m+1]\times[0,0]^{n-m+1}).

From its definition, JJ is an upper order ideal. To show |J|=dn​(S)|J|=d_{n}(S) we will construct a poset isomorphism J≅Dn​(S)J\cong D_{n}(S). If κ∈J\kappa\in J then factor it as a concatenation κ=λ​μ\kappa=\lambda\mu where |λ|=m|\lambda|=m and |μ|=n+1−m|\mu|=n+1-m. Map κ\kappa to κ′=λ′​μ′\kappa^{\prime}=\lambda^{\prime}\mu^{\prime} where λ′\lambda^{\prime} is the sequence obtained from λ\lambda by subtracting 11 from each entry, and μ′=[0,0]n−m\mu^{\prime}=[0,0]^{n-m}. It easy easy to see that this is an isomorphism by constructing the inverse map.

Finally, we have

I∩J=Kn+1(S)∩([1,n−1]×[1,n−2]×⋯×[1,n−m+1]×[2,n−m]×[0,0]n−m+1).I\cap J=K_{n+1}(S)\cap([1,n-1]\times[1,n-2]\times\cdots\times[1,n-m+1]\times[2,n-m]\times[0,0]^{n-m+1}).

Using arguments similar to those in the previous paragraph, one shows that I∩J≅Dn−1​(S)I\cap J\cong D_{n-1}(S) which implies |I∩J|=dn−1​(S)|I\cap J|=d_{n-1}(S). Now we are done by part (b) of the Order Ideal Lemma. ∎

Note that in the special case S=[k]S=[k] we have d⁡(S,n)=(n−1k)d(S;n)=\binom{n-1}{k} since any π∈D⁡(S,n)\pi\in D(S;n) can be formed by putting 11 in the (k+1)(k+1)st position, then choosing kk elements of [2,n][2,n] to put before 11 in decreasing order, and arranging the rest after 11 in increasing order. Thus we have obtained another proof of Corollary 3.2.

6.2 Peak polynomials

We now consider sequences of evaluations of peak polynomials. The peak set of π∈𝔖n\pi\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} is

Pk⁡π={i∣πi−1<πi>πi+1}.\Pk\pi=\{i\mid\pi_{i-1}<\pi_{i}>\pi_{i+1}\}.

Using our canonical example (14) we have

Pk⁡415632={4}.\Pk 415632=\{4\}.

As with the descent set, for a finite set of positive integers SS we let

Pn​(S)={π∈𝔖n∣Pk⁡π=S}.P_{n}(S)=\{\pi\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}\mid\Pk\pi=S\}.

There are some sets SS such that Pn​(S)=∅P_{n}(S)=\emptyset for all n≥0n\geq 0. But if SS does not contain 11 and also does not contain two consecutive integers, one can easily construct π∈𝔖n\pi\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} with Pk⁡π=S\Pk\pi=S if n>max⁡Sn>\max S. We call such SS admissible. The following theorem was proved by Billey, Burdzy, and Sagan [BBS13].

Theorem 6.8.

If SS is admissible then for n>max⁡Sn>\max S we have

#​Pn​(S)=pn​(S)​2n−#​S−1\#P_{n}(S)=p_{n}(S)2^{n-\#S-1}

where pn​(S)p_{n}(S) is a polynomial in nn. ∎

The polynomial pn​(S)p_{n}(S) is called the peak polynomial and more information about these polynomials can be found in [BBPS15, BFT16, DLHIO17, O20, GG21]. We note that the peak set of π\pi can be read off from the descent set since a peak is exactly a non-descent followed by a descent. And the powers of two in #​Pn​(S)\#P_{n}(S) will cancel in a log-concavity inequality. So the proof of the next result closely parallels the one already given for the descent polynomial and the details are omitted.

Theorem 6.9.

If SS is admissible then the sequence (pn​(S))n≥0(p_{n}(S))_{n\geq 0} is log-concave. ∎

6.3 Pattern avoidance

In this subsection we will give a third proof that the Catalan sequence is log-convex, this one using pattern avoidance and the (ordinary) middle order. Say π∈𝔖n\pi\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} contains permutation σ∈𝔖k\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{k} as a classical pattern if there is a subsequence σ′=πi1​πi2​…​πik\sigma^{\prime}=\pi_{i_{1}}\pi_{i_{2}}\ldots\pi_{i_{k}} of π\pi, called a copy, whose elements are in the same relative order as those of σ\sigma. In a bivincular pattern certain pairs of elements of σ′\sigma^{\prime} are specified to be in adjacent positions (indicated by a vertical bar between the two in σ\sigma), or have adjacent values (indicated by a horizontal bar above the smaller of the two in σ\sigma). For example, copies of σ=231\sigma=231 in π=643512\pi=643512 are 451451, 452452, 351351, and 352352. Only one of these is a copy of 2|3​1¯2|3\overline{1} namely 352352. If σ\sigma is any bivincular pattern then its avoidance set is

Avn⁡(σ)={π∈𝔖n∣π contains no copy of σ}.\Av_{n}(\sigma)=\{\pi\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}\mid\text{$\pi$ contains no copy of $\sigma$}\}.

It is well-known that if σ∈𝔖3\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{3} then

#​Avn⁡(σ)=Cn,\#\Av_{n}(\sigma)=C_{n}, (21)

the nnth Catalan number.

The following result of Claesson, Jelínek, and Steingrímsson [CJS12, Lemma 10] will permit us to transfer results from 𝔖n{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} to ℐn{\cal I}_{n}.

Lemma 6.10 ([CJS12]).

For all n≥0n\geq 0, we have π∈Avn⁡(213)\pi\in\Av_{n}(213) if and only if ι⁡(π)\iota(\pi) is weakly increasing. ∎

We can now use (21) to reprove the log-convexity of the Catalan sequence.

Theorem 6.11.

The sequence (#​Avn⁡(213))n≥0=(Cn)n≥0(\#\Av_{n}(213))_{n\geq 0}=(C_{n})_{n\geq 0} is log-convex.

Proof.

We first show that the partial order on Avn⁡(213)\Av_{n}(213) induced from the middle order is a distributive lattice. We claim that this order, is in fact, a sublattice of the middle order of 𝔖n{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} and thus must be distributive. The meet and join of π,σ∈𝔖n\pi,\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} are obtained by taking pairwise minima and maxima of ι⁡(π)\iota(\pi) and ι⁡(σ)\iota(\sigma). From this it is easy to see that if ι⁡(π)\iota(\pi) and ι⁡(σ)\iota(\sigma) are weakly increasing then so are ι⁡(π)∧ι⁡(σ)\iota(\pi)\wedge\iota(\sigma) and ι⁡(π)∨ι⁡(σ)\iota(\pi)\vee\iota(\sigma). The previous lemma completes the proof of the claim.

We now choose two upper order ideals to finish the demonstration of the theorem. We use multiplicity notation for inversion sequences in the usual way. In particular, let

I={ι∈ι⁡(Avn+1⁡(213))∣ι≥(0,1n)},I=\{\iota\in\iota(\Av_{n+1}(213))\mid\iota\geq(0,1^{n})\},

and

J={ι∈ι⁡(Avn+1⁡(213))∣ι≥(0n,n)}.J=\{\iota\in\iota(\Av_{n+1}(213))\mid\iota\geq(0^{n},n)\}.

The verification that these ideals and their intersection have the correct sizes is routine and left to the reader. The Order Ideal Lemma completes the proof. ∎

We note that one can give a similar proof of the log-convexity of the Catalan sequence using middle order restricted to Av⁡(312)\Av(312). One can not apply the same technique to any other permutation π∈𝔖3\pi\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{3} because, as is clear from Figure 8, the restriction of middle order to Av⁡(π)\Av(\pi) is not a distributive lattice.

7 Set partitions

For our last applications of the Order Ideal Lemma, we use set partitions and noncrossing set partitions to prove log-concavity results about Stirling numbers of the second kind and Narayana numbers. In both cases, it will be convenient to express the distributive lattices in terms of restricted growth functions.

7.1 Stirling numbers of the second kind

We first set notation and basic definitions. A set partition of [n][n], β=B1/B2/…/Bk⊢[n]\beta=B_{1}/B_{2}/\ldots/B_{k}\vdash[n], is a family of disjoint subsets BiB_{i} called blocks whose disjoint union is ⊎iBi=[n]\uplus_{i}B_{i}=[n]. In examples, we will eliminate the set braces and commas from the BiB_{i}. We will also always write our partitions in standard form which means that

1=min⁡B1<min⁡B2<…<min⁡Bk.1=\min B_{1}<\min B_{2}<\ldots<\min B_{k}.

For example,

β=12359/46/78⊢[9].\beta=12359/46/78\vdash[9]. (22)

We let

S⁡([n],k)={β∣β⊢[n] with k blocks}.S([n],k)=\{\beta\mid\text{$\beta\vdash[n]$ with $k$ blocks}\}.

The Stirling numbers of the second kind are

S⁡(n,k)=#​S​([n],k).S(n,k)=\#S([n],k).

Set partitions are in bijection with certain sequences called restricted growth functions. A restricted growth function (RGF) is a sequence ρ=ρ1​ρ2​…​ρn\rho=\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\ldots\rho_{n} of positive integers satisfying

  1. 1.

    ρ1=1\rho_{1}=1, and

  2. 2.

    for i≥2i\geq 2 we have

    ρi≤1+max⁡(ρ1​ρ2​…​ρi−1).\rho_{i}\leq 1+\max(\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\ldots\rho_{i-1}).

We call nn the length of ρ\rho and write |ρ|=n|\rho|=n To illustrate

ρ=111212331\rho=111212331 (23)

is an RGF with |ρ|=9|\rho|=9, while τ=111212431\tau=111212431 is not since τ7=4\tau_{7}=4 but 1+max⁡(111212)=31+\max(111212)=3. We will use the notation

RGF⁡(n,k)={ρ∣|ρ|=n​ and ​max⁡ρ=k}.\RGF(n,k)=\{\rho\mid|\rho|=n\text{ and }\max\rho=k\}.

There is a well-known bijection S⁡([n],k)→RGF⁡(n,k)S([n],k)\rightarrow\RGF(n,k) defined by sending β=B1/B2/…/Bk\beta=B_{1}/B_{2}/\ldots/B_{k} to ρ=ρ1​ρ2​…​ρn\rho=\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\ldots\rho_{n} where

ρi=j​ if and only if ​i∈Bj.\rho_{i}=j\text{ if and only if }i\in B_{j}.

The reader can check that the partition in (22) is sent to the RGF in (23) under this map.

To describe the partial order on RGF⁡(n,k)\RGF(n,k) we will need two sequences. If ρ∈RGF⁡(n,k)\rho\in\RGF(n,k) then its sequence of first occurrences (firsts) is

F⁡(ρ)=f1​f2​…​fkF(\rho)=f_{1}f_{2}\ldots f_{k}

defined by

fi=j where ρj is the first i in ρ.f_{i}=\text{$j$ where $\rho_{j}$ is the first $i$ in $\rho$}.

Note that since ρ\rho is an RGF we always have 1=f1<f2<…<fk1=f_{1}<f_{2}<\ldots<f_{k}. We will also use the rest of ρ\rho which is

R⁡(ρ)= ρ with its first occurrences removed.R(\rho)=\text{ $\rho$ with its first occurrences removed}.

Note that |R⁡(ρ)|=n−k|R(\rho)|=n-k. Using our example ρ\rho, we have

F⁡(111212331)=147​ and ​R​(111212331)=111231.F(111212331)=147\text{ and }R(111212331)=111231.

Finally, we define a partial order (RGF⁡(n,k),⪯)(\RGF(n,k),\preceq) by

ρ⪯τ\rho\preceq\tau if and only if F⁡(ρ)≥F⁡(τ)F(\rho)\geq F(\tau) and R⁡(ρ)≤R⁡(τ)R(\rho)\leq R(\tau)

where the orders on FF and RR are component-wise. Figure 9 illustrates this order both on the restricted growth functions ρ∈RGF⁡(4,2)\rho\in\RGF(4,2) on the left and on the pairs (F⁡(ρ),R⁡(ρ))(F(\rho),R(\rho)) on the right.

Lemma 7.1.

The partial order (RGF⁡(n,k),⪯)(\RGF(n,k),\preceq) is a distributive lattice.

Proof.

We first need to prove the existence of meets and joins. As usual, we only do the former as the latter is similar. Recall the definitions of min\min and max\max for integer vectors as given in (19) and (20). We will use the notation F=f1​f2​…​fkF=f_{1}f_{2}\ldots f_{k}, R=r1​r2​…​rn−kR=r_{1}r_{2}\ldots r_{n-k}, and similarly for other first and rest sequences.

Suppose that (F,R)(F,R) and (G,S)(G,S) are two first-rest pairs corresponding to ρ,σ∈RGF⁡(n,k)\rho,\sigma\in\RGF(n,k). If we can show that (F⁡(τ),R⁡(τ))=(max⁡{F,G},min⁡{R,S})(F(\tau),R(\tau))=(\max\{F,G\},\min\{R,S\}) for some τ∈RGF⁡(n,k)\tau\in\RGF(n,k) then it is easy to see that τ\tau is the greatest lower bound of ρ\rho and σ\sigma. The proof that max⁡{F,G}\max\{F,G\} is still an increasing sequence beginning with 11 is easy. So we need to show that if the numbers 1,2,…,k1,2,\ldots,k are placed in min⁡{R,S}\min\{R,S\} at the indices indicated in max⁡{F,G}\max\{F,G\} to form τ\tau, then their positions will be the first occurrences of these numbers. This in turn immediately implies that τ\tau is an RGF. Let us consider what happens when inserting jj. Without loss of generality, suppose that fj≥gjf_{j}\geq g_{j} so that max⁡{fj,gj}=fj\max\{f_{j},g_{j}\}=f_{j}. Now consider any τi\tau_{i} with i<fji<f_{j}. There are now two cases depending on whether τi\tau_{i} is a first occurrence or not. If it is, then τi<j\tau_{i}<j as desired because max⁡{F,G}\max\{F,G\} is increasing. If τi\tau_{i} is not a first occurrence then τi=min⁡{rl,sl}\tau_{i}=\min\{r_{l},s_{l}\} for some l≤il\leq i. So rlr_{l} comes before place fjf_{j} in ρ\rho which is an RGF, and this implies rl<jr_{l}<j. Thus

τi=min⁡{rl,sl}≤rl<j\tau_{i}=\min\{r_{l},s_{l}\}\leq r_{l}<j

which is again what we wanted.

To finish the proof we note, as usual, that distributivity follows from the properties of min\min and max\max. ∎

We now show that a sequence of Stirling numbers of the second kind is log-concave. Note that this sequence is different from the one usually studied where nn is fixed and kk varies which was shown to be log-concave by Lieb [Lie68].

Theorem 7.2.

For any k≥0k\geq 0, the sequence (S⁡(n,k))n≥0(S(n,k))_{n\geq 0} is log-concave.

Proof.

Consider RGF⁡(n+1,k)\RGF(n+1,k) which, by the previous lemma, is a distributive lattice. We first look at the subset given by

I={ρ∈RGF⁡(n+1,k)∣ρ=11​ρ3​…​ρn+1}.I=\{\rho\in\RGF(n+1,k)\mid\rho=11\rho_{3}\ldots\rho_{n+1}\}.

We claim that II is a lower order ideal. For suppose ρ∈I\rho\in I and σ⪯ρ\sigma\preceq\rho. But then we have F⁡(σ)≥F⁡(ρ)=1​f2​…​fkF(\sigma)\geq F(\rho)=1f_{2}\ldots f_{k} where f2≥3f_{2}\geq 3 since ρ\rho begins with two 11’s. It follows that F⁡(σ)=1​g2​…​gkF(\sigma)=1g_{2}\ldots g_{k} where g2≥f2≥3g_{2}\geq f_{2}\geq 3. So, σ\sigma also begins with two 11’s as desired. It should be clear from the definition of an RGF that there is an isomorphism I≅RGF⁡(n,k)I\cong\RGF(n,k) given by removing the first 11 of ρ∈I\rho\in I.

Next consider

J={ρ∈RGF⁡(n+1,k)∣ρ=ρ1​ρ2​…​ρn​k​ and ​n+1∉F⁡(ρ)}.J=\{\rho\in\RGF(n+1,k)\mid\rho=\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\ldots\rho_{n}k\text{ and }n+1\not\in F(\rho)\}.

we wish to show that this is an upper order ideal. So take ρ∈J\rho\in J and σ⪰ρ\sigma\succeq\rho. The two conditions on ρ\rho being in JJ imply that ρn+1=k\rho_{n+1}=k is not a first occurrence. It follows that R⁡(ρ)=r1​r2​…​rn−k​kR(\rho)=r_{1}r_{2}\ldots r_{n-k}k. Now R⁡(σ)≥R⁡(ρ)R(\sigma)\geq R(\rho) implies that R⁡(σ)R(\sigma) also ends with kk. And this means that so does σ\sigma itself, and that this final kk is not a first occurrence since it is from R⁡(σ)R(\sigma). So σ\sigma satisfies the two conditions for inclusion in JJ. There is also an isomorphism J≅RGF⁡(n,k)J\cong\RGF(n,k) gotten by removing the last kk of ρ∈J\rho\in J since that kk is not a first occurrence.

The reader should now find it easy to prove that I∩J≅RGF⁡(n−1,k)I\cap J\cong\RGF(n-1,k). Thus we are done by the Order Ideal Lemma. ∎

7.1.1 Narayana numbers

The Narayana numbers can be defined, for 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n, as

N⁡(n,k)=1n​(nk−1)​(nk).N(n,k)=\frac{1}{n}\binom{n}{k-1}\binom{n}{k}.

They refine the Catalan numbers in that

Cn=∑k=1nN⁡(n,k)C_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}N(n,k)

and count various refinements of the combinatoiral objects enumerated by CnC_{n}. We will prove the log-concavity of sequences of Narayana numbers using their interpretation in terms of non-crossing partitions.

Call a set partition β=B1/B2/…/Bk\beta=B_{1}/B_{2}/\ldots/B_{k} crossing if there exist positive integers a<b<c<da<b<c<d with a,c∈Bia,c\in B_{i} and b,d∈Bjb,d\in B_{j} for some i≠ji\neq j, and non-crossing otherwise. Clearly a partition is non-crossing if and only if the associate restricted growth function ρ=r1​…​rn\rho=r_{1}\ldots r_{n} has no subsequence of the form i​j​i​jijij. We call such RGFs non-crossing as well. For example, in Figure 9 on the left, all the partitions are non-crossing except 12121212. We let

NC⁡(n,k)={ρ∈RGF⁡(n,k)∣ρ is non-crossing}.\NC(n,k)=\{\rho\in\RGF(n,k)\mid\text{$\rho$ is non-crossing}\}.

It is well known that

N⁡(n,k)=#​NC⁡(n,k).N(n,k)=\#\NC(n,k).

Define M⁡(ρ)M(\rho) to be the multiset underlying R⁡(ρ)R(\rho). Using the example from the previous subsection

M⁡(111212331)={{14,2,3}}.M(111212331)=\{\{1^{4},2,3\}\}.

We now partially order NC⁡(n,k)\NC(n,k) by letting ρ​⊴​σ\rho\trianglelefteq\sigma if and only if

F⁡(ρ)≥F⁡(σ)​ and ​M​(ρ)≤M⁡(σ).F(\rho)\geq F(\sigma)\text{ and }M(\rho)\leq M(\sigma). (24)

where we compare two multisets component-wise after writing them out in weakly increasing order. In Figure 10 we have written out the order on NC⁡(4,2)\NC(4,2) in terms of RGFs (left) and (F,M)(F,M) pairs (right).

The following lemma will be useful in proving that the partial order on NC⁡(n,k)\NC(n,k) is a lattice.

Lemma 7.3.

Let F=f1​f2​…​fkF=f_{1}f_{2}\ldots f_{k} be an increasing sequence of integers with f1=1f_{1}=1 and let M={{1m1,2m2,…,kmk}}M=\{\{1^{m_{1}},2^{m_{2}},\ldots,k^{m_{k}}\}\} be a multiset. There is a an RGF ρ\rho with F⁡(ρ)=FF(\rho)=F and M⁡(ρ)=MM(\rho)=M if and only if for all ii with 1<i≤k1<i\leq k we have

fi−i≤m1+m2+⋯+mi−1.f_{i}-i\leq m_{1}+m_{2}+\cdots+m_{i-1}. (25)

Furthermore, there is a unique such non-crossing ρ\rho.

Proof.

Suppose first that ρ\rho exists. Then fi−if_{i}-i is the number places in ρ\rho before fif_{i} which do not contain a first element. And since ρ\rho is an RGF, these places can only contain elements smaller than ii. Since the sum is the total number of elements smaller than ii, the inequality follows.

Now suppose the inequalities hold. We will build the desired RGF ρ\rho. An example of this construction follows the proof. First put 1,2,…,k1,2,\ldots,k in the spaces dictated by FF. Now fill each remaining space from left to right while removing elements from MM as follows. To fill a given space, find the nearest first occurrence from FF to its left, say that is ii. Now pick the largest element of the current version of MM which is at most ii, say that is is j≤ij\leq i. Finally put a jj into the space of ρ\rho and remove a copy of jj from MM. We see from the arguments in the previous paragraph that there will always be an element available to fill the space and so this algorithm terminates with all spaces filled. Furthermore, the RGF restriction is satisfied by construction.

We claim that the RGF ρ\rho constructed in the previous paragraph is noncrossing. Suppose, to the contrary, the it contains a copy of i​j​i​jijij. There are now two cases depending on the relative size of ii and jj. But they are similar so we will only do the case i<ji<j. Note that the second ii and jj in the copy are not first occurrences in ρ\rho and so were added during the procedure using MM. Let kk be the element in a position of FF which is closest on the left to the second ii in i​j​i​jijij. So ii was the largest element of the current MM smaller than or equal to kk. But j>ij>i and, by definition of an RGF and the choice of kk, all elements up to the ii in question are at most kk. In particular j≤kj\leq k because of the first jj in i​j​i​jijij. It follows that there was no jj in MM when the second ii was chosen since the algorithm always picks the largest possible element. But now it is not possible to pick an element in a later place for the second jj.

For uniqueness, suppose that there is another associated noncrossing RGF ρ′\rho^{\prime}. Consider the first place where ρ\rho and ρ′\rho^{\prime} differ and let i′i^{\prime} be the element of ρ′\rho^{\prime} in that place. The elements of FF are the same in both, so i′i^{\prime} must be a place filled by MM in ρ\rho. Let kk be the first occurrence closest to i′i^{\prime} on its left. By definition of how elements are chosen in ρ\rho and the fact that this is the first place where the two RGFs differ, there must be j′∈Mj^{\prime}\in M with i′<j′≤ki^{\prime}<j^{\prime}\leq k which comes later in ρ′\rho^{\prime}. But from what we have established, neither the occurrence of i′i^{\prime}, nor that of j′j^{\prime} is first. It is now easy to see that ρ′\rho^{\prime} has a copy of i′​j′​i′​j′i^{\prime}j^{\prime}i^{\prime}j^{\prime} where the first i′i^{\prime}, j′j^{\prime} are in positions indexed by FF and the second two are as constructed. ∎

To illustrate the building of the RGF ρ\rho in the previous proof, suppose that

(F,M)=(137,{{13,22,3}})(F,M)=(137,\ \{\{1^{3},2^{2},3\}\})

We are to build ρ\rho with |ρ|=|F|+|M|=3+6=9|\rho|=|F|+|M|=3+6=9. We start by putting 1,2,31,2,3 in the spaces dictated by FF to get

ρ=1​_​ 2​_​_​_​ 3​_​_.\rho=1\ \_\ 2\ \_\ \_\ \_\ 3\ \_\ \_.

To fill the first space, we look for the closest first occurrence to its left which is 11. So we must choose the largest element of MM which is at most 11. Of course, this is 11 itself, so moving a 11 from MM to ρ\rho gives

ρ=1 1 2​_​_​_​ 3​_​_​ and ​M={{12,22,3}}.\rho=1\ 1\ 2\ \_\ \_\ \_\ 3\ \_\ \_\text{ and }M=\{\{1^{2},2^{2},3\}\}.

The next space is closest on the left to first occurrence 22. Since MM contains a 22, we move it to ρ\rho to obtain

ρ=1 1 2 2​_​_​ 3​_​_​ and ​M={{12,2,3}}.\rho=1\ 1\ 2\ 2\ \_\ \_\ 3\ \_\ \_\text{ and }M=\{\{1^{2},2,3\}\}.

Similarly the next space is filled with a 22

ρ=1 1 2 2 2​_​ 3​_​_​ and ​M={{12,3}}.\rho=1\ 1\ 2\ 2\ 2\ \_\ 3\ \_\ \_\text{ and }M=\{\{1^{2},3\}\}.

Now MM no longer contains any 22’s so the next space gets the largest element of MM less than 22 which is a 11

ρ=1 1 2 2 2 1 3​_​_​ and ​M={{1,3}}.\rho=1\ 1\ 2\ 2\ 2\ 1\ 3\ \_\ \_\text{ and }M=\{\{1,3\}\}.

The final two spaces have 33 as their closest first occurrence, and both elements of MM are at most 33. So they are added to ρ\rho in decreasing order to finally obtain

ρ=1 1 2 2 2 1 3 3 1.\rho=1\ 1\ 2\ 2\ 2\ 1\ 3\ 3\ 1.

The next lemma will help us show that meets and joins exist in the partial order on NC⁡(n,k)\NC(n,k).

Lemma 7.4.

Let (F,M)(F,M) and (F′,M′)(F^{\prime},M^{\prime}) be set-multiset pairs satisfiying equation (25). Then the pairs (max⁡{F,F′},min⁡{M,M′})(\max\{F,F^{\prime}\},\min\{M,M^{\prime}\}) and (min⁡{F,F′},max⁡{M,M′})(\min\{F,F^{\prime}\},\max\{M,M^{\prime}\}) satisfy the same inequalities.

Proof.

We will only provide the details for (max⁡{F,F′},min⁡{M,M′})(\max\{F,F^{\prime}\},\min\{M,M^{\prime}\}) as the other case is similar. Let F′′=max⁡{F,F′}F^{\prime\prime}=\max\{F,F^{\prime}\} and M′′=min⁡{M,M′}M^{\prime\prime}=\min\{M,M^{\prime}\}. As usual, we use the notation F=f1​f2​…​fkF=f_{1}f_{2}\ldots f_{k}, M={{1m1,2m2,…,kmk}}M=\{\{1^{m_{1}},2^{m_{2}},\ldots,k^{m_{k}}\}\}, and similarly with primes or double primes for the other pairs. Without loss of generality we can assume that fi≥fi′f_{i}\geq f^{\prime}_{i} so that fi′′=fif^{\prime\prime}_{i}=f_{i}. Also M≥M′′M\geq M^{\prime\prime} component wise so that the number of elements less than ii in MM must be at at most their number in M′′M^{\prime\prime}, that is,

m1+m2+⋯+mi−1≤m1′′+m2′′+⋯+mi−1′′.m_{1}+m_{2}+\cdots+m_{i-1}\leq m^{\prime\prime}_{1}+m^{\prime\prime}_{2}+\cdots+m^{\prime\prime}_{i-1}.

Thus

fi′′−i=fi−i≤m1+m2+⋯+mi−1≤m1′′+m2′′+⋯+mi−1′′f^{\prime\prime}_{i}-i=f_{i}-i\leq m_{1}+m_{2}+\cdots+m_{i-1}\leq m^{\prime\prime}_{1}+m^{\prime\prime}_{2}+\cdots+m^{\prime\prime}_{i-1}

as desired. ∎

Lemma 7.5.

The poset (NC⁡(n,k),⊴)(\NC(n,k),\trianglelefteq) is a distributive lattice.

Proof.

Suppose ρ,σ∈NC⁡(n,k)\rho,\sigma\in\NC(n,k). By Lemma 7.3, the pairs (F⁡(ρ),M⁡(ρ))(F(\rho),M(\rho)) and (F⁡(σ),M⁡(σ))(F(\sigma),M(\sigma)) satisfy the inequalities (25). And by the previous lemma, (25) is still satisfied by the pair (max⁡{(F​ρ),F⁡(σ)},min⁡{M⁡(ρ),M⁡(σ)})(\max\{(F\rho),F(\sigma)\},\ \min\{M(\rho),M(\sigma)\}). Using Lemma 7.3 again, there is a unique noncrossing RGF ρ∧σ\rho\wedge\sigma with

F⁡(ρ∧σ)=max⁡{F⁡(ρ),F⁡(σ)}​ and ​M​(ρ∧σ)=min⁡{M⁡(ρ),M⁡(σ)}.F(\rho\wedge\sigma)=\max\{F(\rho),F(\sigma)\}\text{ and }M(\rho\wedge\sigma)=\min\{M(\rho),M(\sigma)\}.

We claim that ρ∧σ\rho\wedge\sigma is the greatest lower bound of ρ\rho and σ\sigma. Indeed, F⁡(ρ∧σ)=max⁡{F⁡(ρ),F⁡(σ)}≥F⁡(ρ),F⁡(σ)F(\rho\wedge\sigma)=\max\{F(\rho),F(\sigma)\}\geq F(\rho),F(\sigma) and M⁡(ρ∧σ)=min⁡{M⁡(ρ),M⁡(σ)}≤M⁡(ρ),M⁡(σ)M(\rho\wedge\sigma)=\min\{M(\rho),M(\sigma)\}\leq M(\rho),M(\sigma) so that ρ∧σ​⊴​ρ,σ\rho\wedge\sigma\trianglelefteq\rho,\sigma by (24). And if τ​⊴​ρ,σ\tau\trianglelefteq\rho,\sigma then F⁡(τ)≥F⁡(ρ),F⁡(σ)F(\tau)\geq F(\rho),F(\sigma) and M⁡(τ)≤M⁡(ρ),M⁡(σ)M(\tau)\leq M(\rho),M(\sigma) by (24) again. So F⁡(τ)≥max⁡{F⁡(ρ),F⁡(σ)}F(\tau)\geq\max\{F(\rho),F(\sigma)\} and M⁡(τ)≤min⁡{M⁡(ρ),M⁡(σ)}M(\tau)\leq\min\{M(\rho),M(\sigma)\}. Using the definition of the partial order one last time we get τ​⊴​ρ∧σ\tau\trianglelefteq\rho\wedge\sigma as desired.

Similarly, one constructs ρ∨σ\rho\vee\sigma as the unique noncrossing RGF with

F⁡(ρ∨σ)=min⁡{F⁡(ρ),F⁡(σ)}​ and ​M​(ρ∨σ)=max⁡{M⁡(ρ),M⁡(σ)}F(\rho\vee\sigma)=\min\{F(\rho),F(\sigma)\}\text{ and }M(\rho\vee\sigma)=\max\{M(\rho),M(\sigma)\}

and shows that it is indeed a least upper bound. The fact that the resulting lattice is distributive follows from the fact that max distributes over min and vice-versa. ∎

We can finally prove our main result of this subsection.

Theorem 7.6.

For fixed kk, the sequence of Narayana numbers (N⁡(n,k))n≥0(N(n,k))_{n\geq 0} is log-concave.

Proof.

Throughout this proof we will consider the elements ρ∈NC⁡(n,k)\rho\in\NC(n,k) as set-multiset ordered pairs (F⁡(ρ),M⁡(ρ))(F(\rho),M(\rho)) where F⁡(ρ)=f1​f2​…​fkF(\rho)=f_{1}f_{2}\ldots f_{k} and M⁡(ρ)={{1m1,2m2,…,kmk}}M(\rho)=\{\{1^{m_{1}},2^{m_{2}},\ldots,k^{m_{k}}\}\}.

Consider the subset of NC⁡(n+1,k)\NC(n+1,k) given by

I={(F,M)∈NC⁡(n+1,k)∣f2≥3}.I=\{(F,M)\in\NC(n+1,k)\mid f_{2}\geq 3\}.

Note that II is a lower order ideal since if (F,M)∈I(F,M)\in I and (F′,M′)≤(F,M)(F^{\prime},M^{\prime})\leq(F,M) then F′≥FF^{\prime}\geq F. It follows that f2′≥f3≥3f_{2}^{\prime}\geq f_{3}\geq 3 so that (F′,M′)∈I(F^{\prime},M^{\prime})\in I. We also claim that I≅NC⁡(n,k)I\cong\NC(n,k). If (F,M)∈I(F,M)\in I then f2≥3f_{2}\geq 3. Thus ρ\rho, the associated RGF, must begin with at least two 11’s. This forces m1≥1m_{1}\geq 1. Now map (F,M)(F,M) to the pair (F′,M′)(F^{\prime},M^{\prime}) where

fi′={1if i=1,fi−1if i≥2,f_{i}^{\prime}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}1&\mbox{if $i=1$,}\\ f_{i}-1&\mbox{if $i\geq 2$,}\end{array}\right.

and

mi′={m1−1if i=1,miif i≥2.m_{i}^{\prime}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}m_{1}-1&\mbox{if $i=1$,}\\ m_{i}&\mbox{if $i\geq 2$.}\end{array}\right.

It is easy to check that this gives an isomorphism. So we have #​I=N⁡(n,k)\#I=N(n,k).

Now define

J={(F,M)∈NC⁡(n+1,k)∣mk≥1}.J=\{(F,M)\in\NC(n+1,k)\mid m_{k}\geq 1\}.

This forces JJ to be an upper order ideal, for suppose (F,M)∈J(F,M)\in J and (F′,M′)≥(F,M)(F^{\prime},M^{\prime})\geq(F,M). Since mk≥1m_{k}\geq 1, the nondecreasing rearrangement of MM must end in kk. So M′≥MM^{\prime}\geq M means the same is true for M′M^{\prime}, and mk′≥1m_{k}^{\prime}\geq 1. Again, there is an isomorphism between JJ and NC⁡(n,k)\NC(n,k). The fact that mk≥1m_{k}\geq 1 implies fk≤nf_{k}\leq n since there are at least two kk’s in the associated ρ\rho and so the first one can not be in the final position n+1n+1. So the following function is well defined. Map (F,M)(F,M) to (F′,M′)(F^{\prime},M^{\prime}) where F′=FF^{\prime}=F and

mi′={mk−1if i=k,miif i<k.m_{i}^{\prime}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}m_{k}-1&\mbox{if $i=k$,}\\ m_{i}&\mbox{if $i<k$.}\end{array}\right.

Again, it is not hard to show that this is an isomorphism. The fact that I∩J≅NC⁡(n−1,k)I\cap J\cong\NC(n-1,k) is similarly left to the reader. ∎

8 Future directions

The purpose of this section is threefold. First, we will give a proof of the Order Ideal Lemma using the FKG inequality. Next, we will describe various sequences to which it might be possible to apply our method but which have so far resisted proof. Finally, we end with some possible avenues for extending the Order Ideal Lemma.

8.1 Proof of the Order Ideal Lemma

Let ℝ≥0{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} denote the nonnegative real numbers. For any poset (P,⪯)(P,\preceq) we call a function f:P→ℝ≥0f:P\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} increasing if

x⪯y​ implies ​f​(x)≤f⁡(y).x\preceq y\text{ implies }f(x)\leq f(y).

Similarly define ff to be decreasing. Now suppose (L,⪯)(L,\preceq) is a lattice. A function μ:L→ℝ≥0\mu:L\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is log-supermodular if for all x,y∈Lx,y\in L we have

μ⁡(x)​μ​(y)≤μ⁡(x∧y)​μ​(x∨y).\mu(x)\mu(y)\leq\mu(x\land y)\mu(x\lor y).

Finally, given a function f:L→ℝ≥0f:L\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} and a log-supermodular function μ:L→ℝ≥0\mu:L\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, we use the notation

S⁡(f)=∑x∈Lf⁡(x)​μ​(x).S(f)=\sum_{x\in L}f(x)\mu(x).

In particular, if g:L→ℝ≥0g:L\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} is another function then

S⁡(f​g)=∑x∈Lf⁡(x)​g​(x)​μ​(x),S(fg)=\sum_{x\in L}f(x)g(x)\mu(x),

and, letting 𝟏:L→ℝ≥0{\bf 1}:L\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} be the function defined by 𝟏​(x)=1{\bf 1}(x)=1 for all x∈Lx\in L,

S⁡(𝟏)=∑x∈Lμ⁡(x).S({\bf 1})=\sum_{x\in L}\mu(x).

We can now state the FKG inequality [FKG71].

Theorem 8.1 ([FKG71]).

Suppose (L,⪯)(L,\preceq) is a finite distributive lattice and μ:L→ℝ≥0\mu:L\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is a log-supermodular function. Suppose also that f,g:L→ℝ≥0f,g:L\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} are two functions.

  1. (a)

    If f,gf,g are both increasing or both decreasing then

    S⁡(f)⋅S⁡(g)≤S⁡(f​g)⋅S⁡(𝟏).S(f)\cdot S(g)\leq S(fg)\cdot S({\bf 1}).
  2. (b)

    If one of f,gf,g is increasing and the other decreasing then

     ​S​(f)⋅S⁡(g)≥S⁡(f​g)⋅S⁡(𝟏).∎\rule{4.30554pt}{0.0pt}\hfill{\displaystyle S(f)\cdot S(g)\geq S(fg)\cdot S({\bf 1}).}\hfill\qed

The Order Ideal Lemma, which is restated here for convenience, is a corollary.

Lemma 8.2 (The Order Ideal Lemma).

Let LL be a distributive lattice and suppose that I,J⊆LI,J\subseteq L are ideals.

  1. (a)

    If I,JI,J are both lower ideals or both upper ideals then

    |I|⋅|J|≤|I∩J|⋅|L|.|I|\cdot|J|\leq|I\cap J|\cdot|L|.
  2. (b)

    If one of I,JI,J is a lower order ideal and the other is upper then

    |I|⋅|J|≥|I∩J|⋅|L|.|I|\cdot|J|\geq|I\cap J|\cdot|L|.
Proof.

We will prove (b) as (a) is similar. Suppose that II is the lower order ideal and JJ is the upper. Define indicator functions f,g:L→ℝ≥0f,g:L\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} by

f⁡(x)={1if x∈I,0else,f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}1&\mbox{if $x\in I$,}\\ 0&\mbox{else,}\end{array}\right.

and

g⁡(x)={1if x∈J,0else.g(x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}1&\mbox{if $x\in J$,}\\ 0&\mbox{else.}\end{array}\right.
