Since II is a lower order ideal we have that ff is decreasing and, by the same token, gg is increasing. Also define μ=𝟏\mu={\bf 1} which is clearly log-supermodular. Now, by the FKG Theorem, part (b),

|I|⋅|J|=S⁡(f)⋅S⁡(g)≥S⁡(f​g)⋅S⁡(𝟏)=|I∩J|⋅|L||I|\cdot|J|=S(f)\cdot S(g)\geq S(fg)\cdot S({\bf 1})=|I\cap J|\cdot|L|

which finishes the proof. ∎

8.2 Other sequences

In this subsection we discuss various sequences to which we hope the Order Ideal Lemma might be applied.

A superset of the set of permutations (viewed as permutations matrices) is the set of alternating sign matrices. An alternating sign matrix or ASM is a matrix such that

  1. 1.

    every entry is ±1\pm 1 or 00, and

  2. 2.

    in each row and each column the nonzero entries alternate 11 and −1-1, beginning and ending with 11.

The number of n×nn\times n ASM’s is given by

asmn=∏i=0n−1(3​i+1)!(n+i)!.\asm_{n}=\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}\frac{(3i+1)!}{(n+i)!}.

This formula was conjectured by Mills, Robbins, and Rumsey in 1983 [MRR83] and then given two proofs in 1996, the first by Zeilberger [Zei96] and the second by Kuperberg [Kup96]. The same numbers count descending plane partitions, totally symmetric self-complementary plane partitions, configurations of square ice with domain wall boundary conditions, and various other mathematical objects. Using cancellation of factorials, it is easy to prove the following result.

Theorem 8.3.

The sequence (asmn)n≥0(\asm_{n})_{n\geq 0} is log-convex. ∎

It is a natural question to find a proof of the previous resul using the Order Ideal Lemma and this has been done by Fischer, Konvalinka, Sagan, and Weigandt [FKSW26] using the corresponding corner sum matrices. These ideas can also be used to prove log-concavity and log-convexity for related objects which do not have a nice product formula.

A famous set of permutations of a multiset is the set of parking functions. A parking function of length nn is a sequence of integers ϕ=ϕ1​ϕ2​…​ϕn\phi=\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\ldots\phi_{n} whose weakly increasing rearrangement ψ=ψ1​ψ2​…​ψn\psi=\psi_{1}\psi_{2}\ldots\psi_{n} satisfies

1≤ψi≤i1\leq\psi_{i}\leq i

for i∈[n]i\in[n]. Otherwise put, and using the notation of (5) and (15), ψ−1∈ℐn\psi-1\in{\cal I}_{n}. Parking functions were first defined by Konheim and Weiss [KW66] and have since been widely studied, in part because of their connections with noncrossing partitions, hyperplane arrangements, and other combinatorial constructs. The number of parking functions of length nn is given by

pfn=(n+1)n−1.\prf_{n}=(n+1)^{n-1}.

We note that this is also the number of labeled trees on n+1n+1 vertices. The next result follows from an algebraicly derived theorem of Chen, Wang, and Yang [CWY11] about strongly qq-log-concave sequences (see the next section for the definition) applied to certain rooted trees.

Theorem 8.4 ([CWY11]).

The sequence (nn−1)n≥2(n^{n-1})_{n\geq 2} is log-convex. ∎

Using simple division and the result just given, we obtain the following.

Theorem 8.5 ([CWY11]).

The sequence (pfn)n≥1(\prf_{n})_{n\geq 1} is log-convex. ∎

It would be very interesting to give a combinatorial proof of this theorem using the Order Ideal Lemma. Unfortunately, we have been unable to find the appropriate distributive lattice.

Given a permutation, one can look at the values of the peaks rather than their indices. Specifically, the pinnacle set of π∈𝔖n\pi\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} is

Pin⁡π={πi∣πi−1<πi>πi1}.\Pin\pi=\{\pi_{i}\mid\pi_{i-1}<\pi_{i}>\pi_{i_{1}}\}.

Pinnacle sets were first studied by Strehl [Str78] although he called them peak sets. They were then rediscovered by Davis, Nelson, Petersen, and Tenner [DNKPT18] and have since been studied by a number of authors [Rus20, DLHH+21, RT21, Fan22, DLM+22, Min23, FNT24]. Interestingly, they do not behave like peaks. For example, there does not seem to be any corresponding pinnacle polynomial.

Since pinnacles involve permutation values, it is natural to try and study them using the ordinary middle order. However, the posets obtained by restricting this order to all permutations with a given length and pinnacle set do not always have connected Hasse diagrams. Instead, consider the following variant which has occurred, for example, in the work of Rusu and Tenner [RT21]. Let σ\sigma be a permutation of distinct positive integers. Let

Pinn⁡(σ)={π∈𝔖n∣the pinnacles of π are the elements of σ in that order}.\Pin_{n}(\sigma)=\{\pi\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}\mid\text{the pinnacles of $\pi$ are the elements of $\sigma$ in that order}\}.

and

pinn⁡(σ)=#​Pinn⁡(σ).\pin_{n}(\sigma)=\#\Pin_{n}(\sigma).

Computation of examples raise the following questions.

Question 8.6.

For all nn and σ\sigma:

  1. (a)

    Is the restriction of the middle order to Pinn⁡(σ)\Pin_{n}(\sigma) a distributive lattice?

  2. (b)

    Is the sequence (pinn⁡(σ))(\pin_{n}(\sigma)) log-concave?

It would be interesting if one could apply our methods to prove log-convexity of other pattern avoidance sequences. In fact, they are conjectured to satisfy a stronger property. Call (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} a Stieltjes moment sequence if there exists a nonnegative measure μ\mu supported on [0,∞)[0,\infty) such that

an=∫0∞xn​𝑑μ​(x)a_{n}=\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{n}d\mu(x)

for all n≥0n\geq 0. This is equivalent to requiring that all of the determinants of the Hankel matrix

H=[ai+j]i,j∈ℕ=[a0a1a2⋯a1a2a3⋯a2a3a4⋯⋮⋮⋮⋱]H=[a_{i+j}]_{i,j\in{\mathbb{N}}}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cccc}a_{0}&a_{1}&a_{2}&\cdots\\ a_{1}&a_{2}&a_{3}&\cdots\\ a_{2}&a_{3}&a_{4}&\cdots\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots\end{array}\right]

are non-negative. Note that this immediately implies log-convexity by taking adjacent 2×22\times 2 minors. In his thesis, Elvey Price posed the following question.

Question 8.7 ([Elv18]).

Suppose σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} for n≥2n\geq 2. Is the sequence (#​Avn⁡(σ))n≥0(\#\Av_{n}(\sigma))_{n\geq 0} always a Stieltjes moment sequence?

It is known that the answer to this question is “yes” for all σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} where 2≤n≤42\leq n\leq 4 except possibly σ=1324\sigma=1324 and the other σ\sigma giving the same avoidance sequence. See the article of Vatter [Vat26] for details as well as more intriguing open questions related to pattern avoidance.

Finally, given the nice behaviour of the Stirling numbers of the second kind, one could ask what happens with those of the first. Recall that the signless Stirling numbers of the first kind are

c⁡(n,k)=#⁡{π∈𝔖n∣π has k cycles in its disjoint cycle decomposition}.c(n,k)=\#\{\pi\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}\mid\text{$\pi$ has $k$ cycles in its disjoint cycle decomposition}\}.

We have checked the following conjecture for 1≤k≤n≤1001\leq k\leq n\leq 100.

Conjecture 8.8.

Given kk, there is an integer NkN_{k} such that (c⁡(n,k))n≥0(c(n,k))_{n\geq 0} is log-concave for n<Nkn<N_{k} and log-convex for n≥Nkn\geq N_{k}.

8.3 qq-analogues, 𝐱{\bf x}-analogues, and total positivity

Let qq be a variable. There is a qq-analogue of the FKG inequality which makes it possible to prove generalizations of our results in a straightforward manner. Put a partial order ≤\leq on the polynomial algebra ℝ⁡[q]{\mathbb{R}}[q] by defining

p⁡(q)≤s⁡(q)​ if and only if ​s​(q)−p⁡(q)∈ℝ≥0​[q].p(q)\leq s(q)\text{ if and only if }s(q)-p(q)\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}[q]. (26)

We can now define a sequence of such polynomials (pn​(q))n≥0(p_{n}(q))_{n\geq 0} to be qq-log-concave if

pn​(q)2≥pn−1​(q)​pn+1​(q)p_{n}(q)^{2}\geq p_{n-1}(q)p_{n+1}(q)

for all n≥1n\geq 1 and similarly for qq-log-convexity.

Suppose (L,⪯)(L,\preceq) is a lattice and ℕ{\mathbb{N}} is the nonnegative integers. Call a function r:L→ℕr:L\rightarrow{\mathbb{N}} modular if

r⁡(x)+r⁡(y)=r⁡(x∧y)+f⁡(x∨y).r(x)+r(y)=r(x\wedge y)+f(x\vee y).

If LL is distributive, then it has a rank function which is an example of a modular function. If, in addition to rr, we have a function f:L→ℝ≥0f:L\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} and a log-supermodular function μ:L→ℝ≥0\mu:L\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} then we have an associated polynomial

S⁡[f]=∑x∈Lf⁡(x)​μ​(x)​qr⁡(x).S[f]=\sum_{x\in L}f(x)\mu(x)q^{r(x)}.

The following result was proved by Björner [Bj11] for the rank function. Then Chen, Pak, and Panova [CPP23] noted that the same proof would work for any modular function.

Theorem 8.9 ([Bj11, CPP23]).

Suppose (L,⪯)(L,\preceq) is a finite distributive lattice, μ:L→ℝ≥0\mu:L\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is a log-supermodular function, and r:L→ℕr:L\rightarrow{\mathbb{N}} is modular. Suppose also that f,g:L→ℝ≥0f,g:L\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} are two functions.

  1. (a)

    If f,gf,g are both increasing or both decreasing then

    S⁡[f]⋅S⁡[g]≤S⁡[f​g]⋅S⁡[𝟏].S[f]\cdot S[g]\leq S[fg]\cdot S[{\bf 1}].
  2. (b)

    If one of f,gf,g is increasing and the other decreasing then

     ​S​[f]⋅S⁡[g]≥S⁡[f​g]⋅S⁡[𝟏].∎\rule{4.30554pt}{0.0pt}\hfill{\displaystyle S[f]\cdot S[g]\geq S[fg]\cdot S[{\bf 1}].}\hfill\qed

The following qq-analogue of the Order Ideal Lemma follows from the previous theorem in much the same way that the original result follows from the FKG inequality. So the demonstration is omitted. For a modular function rr will use the notation

[I]q=∑x∈Iqr⁡(x).[I]_{q}=\sum_{x\in I}q^{r(x)}.
Lemma 8.10 (The qq-Order Ideal Lemma).

Let LL be a distributive lattice, r:L→ℕr:L\rightarrow{\mathbb{N}} be modular, and suppose that I,J⊆LI,J\subseteq L are ideals.

  1. (a)

    If I,JI,J are both lower ideals or both upper ideals then

    [I]q⋅[J]q≤[I∩J]q⋅[L]q.[I]_{q}\cdot[J]_{q}\leq[I\cap J]_{q}\cdot[L]_{q}.
  2. (b)

    If one of I,JI,J is a lower order ideal and the other is upper then

     ​[I]q⋅[J]q≥[I∩J]q⋅[L]q.∎\rule{4.30554pt}{0.0pt}\hfill{\displaystyle[I]_{q}\cdot[J]_{q}\geq[I\cap J]_{q}\cdot[L]_{q}.}\hfill\qed

We now show how to use the qq-Order Ideal Lemma to obtain a generalization of Theorem 4.3 to principal specializations of Schur functions, noting that a similar extension works for the more general Theorem 4.2.

Theorem 8.11.

For any partition λ\lambda the sequence (sλ​(q,q2,…,qn))n≥0(s_{\lambda}(q,q^{2},\ldots,q^{n}))_{n\geq 0} is qq-log-concave.

Proof.

For an SSYT TT of shape λ\lambda we let

r⁡(T)=∑(i,j)∈λTi,j.r(T)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\lambda}T_{i,j}.

Note that this is a modular function since the meet and join of tableaux are obtained by taking element-wise minima and maxima, and for any real numbers x,yx,y we have

x+y=min⁡{x,y}+max⁡{x,y}x+y=\min\{x,y\}+\max\{x,y\}

Letting

SSYTλ⁡(n)={T∈SSYTλ∣max⁡T≤n}\SSYT_{\lambda}(n)=\{T\in\SSYT_{\lambda}\mid\max T\leq n\}

we have

sλ​(q,q2,…,qn)=∑T∈SSYTλ⁡(n)∏(i,j)∈λqTi,j=∑T∈SSYTλ⁡(n)qr⁡(T).s_{\lambda}(q,q^{2},\ldots,q^{n})=\sum_{T\in\SSYT_{\lambda}(n)}\ \prod_{(i,j)\in\lambda}q^{T_{i,j}}=\sum_{T\in\SSYT_{\lambda}(n)}q^{r(T)}.

Now using using the lower order ideal

I={T∈SSYTλ⁡(n+1)∣max⁡T≤n},I=\{T\in\SSYT_{\lambda}(n+1)\mid\max T\leq n\},

the upper order ideal

J={T∈SSYTλ⁡(n+1)∣min⁡T≥2},J=\{T\in\SSYT_{\lambda}(n+1)\mid\min T\geq 2\},

and the qq-Order Ideal Lemma completes the proof. ∎

There is an extension of qq-log-concavity to several variables which would also be worth considering. Suppose that we have a sequence of positive real numbers (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} which is log concave. Rewriting the inequalities gives

a0a1≤a1a2≤a2a3≤….\frac{a_{0}}{a_{1}}\leq\frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}}\leq\frac{a_{2}}{a_{3}}\leq\ldots\ .

Now cross-multiplying any two fractions gives the seemingly stronger, but actually equivalent, condition that

am​an≥am−1​an+1a_{m}a_{n}\geq a_{m-1}a_{n+1}

for all 0<m≤n0<m\leq n. We note that the analogous inequalities for polynomials in qq are not equivalent to qq-log-concavity and are called strong qq-log-concavity.

Suppose that ≤\leq is a partial order on the polynomial ring ℝ⁡[𝐱]{\mathbb{R}}[{\bf x}] where 𝐱={x1,x2,…}{\bf x}=\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots\}. Say that this order is standard if it satisfies the following three axioms.

  1. 1.

    If f​(𝐱)∈ℝ≥0​[𝐱]f({\bf x})\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}[{\bf x}] then f⁡(𝐱)≥0f({\bf x})\geq 0.

  2. 2.

    If f⁡(𝐱)≤g⁡(𝐱)f({\bf x})\leq g({\bf x}) then f⁡(𝐱)+h⁡(𝐱)≤g⁡(𝐱)+h⁡(𝐱)f({\bf x})+h({\bf x})\leq g({\bf x})+h({\bf x}) for all h⁡(𝐱)∈ℝ⁡[𝐱]h({\bf x})\in{\mathbb{R}}[{\bf x}].

  3. 3.

    If f⁡(𝐱)≤g⁡(𝐱)f({\bf x})\leq g({\bf x}) then f⁡(𝐱)​h​(𝐱)≤g⁡(𝐱)​h​(𝐱)f({\bf x})h({\bf x})\leq g({\bf x})h({\bf x}) for all h​(𝐱)∈ℝ≥0​[𝐱]h({\bf x})\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}[{\bf x}].

Note that the order defined by (26) with qq replaced by 𝐱{\bf x} everywhere is standard. Call a sequence (fn​(𝐱))n≥0(f_{n}({\bf x}))_{n\geq 0} strongly 𝐱{\bf x}-log-concave with respect to a standard partial order if, for all 0<m≤n0<m\leq n, we have

fm​(𝐱)​fn​(𝐱)≥fm−1​(𝐱)​fn+1​(𝐱).f_{m}({\bf x})f_{n}({\bf x})\geq f_{m-1}({\bf x})f_{n+1}({\bf x}).

Sagan [Sag92] proved the following result.

Theorem 8.12 ([Sag92]).

Fix k≥0k\geq 0 and let ≤\leq be a standard partial order on ℝ⁡[𝐱]{\mathbb{R}}[{\bf x}]. If the sequence (xn)n≥0(x_{n})_{n\geq 0} is strongly 𝐱{\bf x}-log-concave then so are the sequences

(ek​(x1,x2,…,xn))n≥0​ and ​(hk​(x1,x2,…,xn))n≥0(e_{k}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}))_{n\geq 0}\text{ and }(h_{k}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}))_{n\geq 0}

where eke_{k} and hkh_{k} are the kkth elementary and complete homogeneous symmetric functions, respectively. ∎

We note that Chan and Pak [CP23, Theorem 6.1] have proved a multivariate version of the Ahlswede Daykin (AD) inequality [AD78]. Since the ordinary AD inequality can be used to prove FKG, the Chan-Pak result implies a multivariate analogue of the Order Ideal Lemma which could yield interesting results.

It would be very interesting to prove an 𝐱{\bf x}-analogue of the FKG inequality and apply it to prove (strong) 𝐱{\bf x}-log-concavity and 𝐱{\bf x}-log-convexity results.

Another way to generalized our results would be in terms of total positivity. Note that we can rewrite the log-concavity of a real sequence (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} in terms of a determinant

|anan+1an−1an|≥0.\left|\begin{array}[]{cc}a_{n}&a_{n+1}\\ a_{n-1}&a_{n}\end{array}\right|\geq 0.

Letting an=0a_{n}=0 for n<0n<0, consider the infinite Toeplitz matrix

T=[aj−i]i,j∈ℕ=[a0a1a2⋯0a0a1⋯00a0⋯⋮⋮⋮⋱].T=[a_{j-i}]_{i,j\in{\mathbb{N}}}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cccc}a_{0}&a_{1}&a_{2}&\cdots\\ 0&a_{0}&a_{1}&\cdots\\ 0&0&a_{0}&\cdots\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots\end{array}\right].

Call (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} totally positive if all minors of TT are nonnegative. Note that this implies log-concavity because of the connected 2×22\times 2 minors (that is, those consisting of two adjacent rows and two adjacent columns). It would be very interesting to find an extension of the FKG inequality and the Order Ideal Lemma which could be used to prove total positivity.
